title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: You may find yourself admiring this tower of granite, which has withstood the challenges of many ages. However, it is worth considering that this impressive structure was constructed by a small, skilled hand, suggesting that the creator may hold more significance than the creation itself. The hand that built the tower can often dismantle it even more swiftly. Perhaps more important than the hand is the unseen thought that guided its construction; behind every rough outcome, there tends to be a finer cause. When examined closely, what we perceive as permanent might reveal its underlying secrets. For instance, a considerable estate might seem like a solid and enduring fact to women and children, yet to a merchant, it may appear as something easily formed from various materials and just as easily lost. An orchard, well-tended land, and favorable conditions may seem like fixed assets to a city dweller, but to a larger farmer, they are often as changeable as the harvest. Nature may give the impression of stability, but it too has causes that can be understood, leading one to question whether these expansive fields and distinctive leaves truly remain so unchanging. The concept of permanence can vary in meaning. Everything exists in a state of flux. Just as moons do not limit spiritual power, neither do other tangible objects.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: People may think that when you reject popular standards, you are rejecting all standards and simply embracing lawlessness; and a bold, pleasure-seeking person may use the name of philosophy to make his crimes seem respectable. But the law of consciousness remains. There are two confessionals, and in one or the other we must be absolved. You may complete your round of duties by clearing yourself in the direct way or in the reflective way. Consider whether you have satisfied your relations to father, mother, cousin, neighbor, town, cat, and dog; whether any of these can rightly blame you. But I may also neglect this reflective standard and absolve myself to myself. I have my own strict claims and my own complete circle. It denies the name of duty to many offices that are called duties. Yet if I can pay its debts, it allows me to dispense with the popular code. If anyone imagines that this law is lax, let him keep its commandment for one day. In short, while others may mistake self-rule for lawlessness, the law of consciousness still holds, and it can either replace or confirm the ordinary code depending on how faithfully we meet its demands.

You may fulfill your round of duties by clearing yourself in the direct, or in the reflex way. But if I can discharge its debts, it enables me to dispense with the popular code. If any one imagines that this law is lax, let him keep its commandment one day.

In short, while others might see self-control as being wild, the law of consciousness is still in place. It can either take over or support the usual rules, depending on how well you follow it.

title: Essays by Ralph Waldo Emerson
input: We require books that possess this profound cathartic quality far more than we require books focused on political science or private economics. Life presents itself as a celebration solely to the wise. When viewed from the perspective of prudence, it reveals a tattered and perilous facade. The transgressions against the laws of nature committed by both our predecessors and contemporaries result in consequences that affect us as well. The presence of disease and deformity in our environment serves as a testament to the violations of natural, intellectual, and moral laws, often compounding these violations to generate pervasive suffering. Conditions such as tetanus that contorts an individual’s posture, rabies that induces irrational behavior towards loved ones, and madness that leads to bizarre eating habits—along with war, plague, cholera, and famine—reflect a certain brutality inherent in nature. This brutality, having originated from human wrongdoing, must manifest itself through human suffering. Unfortunately, it is noteworthy that nearly every individual has, to some degree, become a participant in this collective wrongdoing, thereby rendering themselves liable for a share in the subsequent atonement.

Seen from the nook and chimney-side of prudence, it wears a ragged and dangerous front. The violations of the laws of nature by our predecessors and our contemporaries are punished in us also. The disease and deformity around us certify the infraction of natural, intellectual, and moral laws, and often violation on violation to breed such compound misery. A lockjaw that bends a man's head back to his heels, hydrophobia that makes him bark at his wife and babes, insanity that makes him eat grass; war, plague, cholera, famine indicate a certain ferocity in nature, which, as it had its inlet by human crime, must have its outlet by human suffering. Unhappily, almost no man exists who has not in his own person become, to some amount, a stockholder in the sin, and so made himself liable to a share in the expiation.

The mistakes people before and now have made against nature’s rules affect us too. Disease and bad looks around us show how people have broken natural, smart, and moral rules. These breaks make more suffering. Things like tetanus that twist someone’s body, rabies that makes people act strangely towards family, madness that leads to odd eating—plus war, plague, cholera, and famine—show nature’s rough side. This roughness came from people’s bad actions, so it must come through people’s pain. Sadly, most people have done some of this wrong, so they’re part of the trouble and must face some of the punishment.

The offences against the laws of nature committed by our ancestors and ourselves have consequences that reach to us. The disease and deformity which surround us, are the fruits of the violation of the laws of nature, of the intellect, of the morals; and these violations, multiplied together, produce an all-pervading misery. Tetanus, which bows the posture of the body, rabies, which makes men spit at their parents, madness, which makes them eat vegetables, war, plague, cholera, famine, are the fruits of a certain cruelty of nature. Cruelty which has been the fruit of human vice, must appear in human wretchedness. And it is to be regretted that nearly every one has become in some degree a party to the general vice, and is liable to a share of the future punishment.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
input:
Upon arriving home, he noticed that his servant was still awake, waiting for him. He instructed the servant to rest and then settled onto the sofa in the library, reflecting on some of the remarks made by Lord Henry. 

He began to question whether it was indeed true that one could never change. A deep yearning for the innocence of his youth surfaced—his pure, unblemished boyhood, as Lord Henry had referred to it. He was aware that he had compromised himself, allowing corruption to infiltrate his thoughts and instilling a sense of horror in his imagination; he recognized that he had negatively influenced others and had taken a troubling pleasure in doing so. Among the lives he had interacted with, it was those with the greatest potential that he had led to disappointment. Yet, he wondered if all was lost. Was there no possibility for redemption?
human:
When he reached home, he found his servant waiting up for him. He sent him to bed, and threw himself down on the sofa in the library, and began to think over some of the things that Lord Henry had said to him.

Was it really true that one could never change? He felt a wild longing for the unstained purity of his boyhood - his rose-white boyhood, as Lord Henry had once called it. He knew that he had tarnished himself, filled his mind with corruption and given horror to his fancy; that he had been an evil influence to others, and had experienced a terrible joy in being so; and that of the lives that had crossed his own, it had been the fairest and the most full of promise that he had brought to shame. But was it all irretrievable? Was there no hope for him?

He started to wonder if really, you could never change. A feeling came over him for the innocence of his young days—the pure, clean boyhood Lord Henry had called it. He knew he had let things go, let corruption creep into his mind and made his imagination full of fear. He knew he had hurt others, that he had enjoyed making them unhappy. Among the people he had met, it was the ones with the most promise he had let down. Yet he wondered if everything was gone. Was there any hope left?

He bade him rest, and then, sitting down on the sofa in the library, began to wonder whether it was true that one could never change. A longing for the purity of his childhood came upon him - his beautiful, unstained boyhood as Lord Henry had called it. He knew that he had corrupted himself, that corruption had crept into his mind and made him afraid; he knew that he had spoilt others and that he had derived a sick pleasure from spoiling them; among the lives that he had touched it was the lives of those most likely to be good that had been spoiled; but was everything over? Could nothing be saved?

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
input: The worship of the senses has often been criticized, as many people instinctively fear passions and sensations that seem more powerful than themselves, sensations shared with less complex forms of life. However, Dorian Gray believed that the true essence of the senses had not been fully grasped. He thought they had remained primitive and animalistic because society attempted to suppress or punish them, rather than nurturing them as components of a new spirituality characterized by an appreciation for beauty. Reflecting on humanity's journey through history, he felt a profound sense of loss. Much had been sacrificed with little benefit, leading to extreme rejection of pleasure and painful self-denial. These responses stemmed from fear and resulted in a degradation that was far worse than the imagined decline they sought to avoid. Nature, in its ironic way, drove the ascetic into the wild, providing him with animals as companions instead of fellow humans.
human: The worship of the senses has often, and with much justice, been decried, men feeling a natural instinct of terror about passions and sensations that seem stronger than themselves, and that they are conscious of sharing with the less highly organized forms of existence. But it appeared to Dorian Gray that the true nature of the senses had never been understood, and that they had remained savage and animal merely because the world had sought to starve them into submission or to kill them by pain, instead of aiming at making them elements of a new spirituality, of which a fine instinct for beauty was to be the dominant characteristic. As he looked back upon man moving through history, he was haunted by a feeling of loss. So much had been surrendered! and to such little purpose! There had been mad wilful rejections, monstrous forms of self-torture and self-denial, whose origin was fear and whose result was a degradation infinitely more terrible than that fancied degradation from which, in their ignorance, they had sought to escape; Nature, in her wonderful irony, driving out the anchorite to feed with the wild animals of the desert and giving to the hermit the beasts of the field as his companions.
base: The worship of the senses has been criticized often. People fear passions and sensations that feel stronger than themselves, things shared with simpler lives. Dorian Gray thought the real nature of the senses wasn't understood. He believed they stayed wild and animal because society tried to stop them, not help them grow into something new, a kind of spirit that values beauty. Looking back at history, he felt deep sorrow. A lot was given for little return, leading to harsh rejection of pleasure and strict self-denial. These reactions came from fear and caused a fall worse than what they tried to prevent. Nature, in its own way, pushed the ascetic into the wild, giving him animals as friends instead of people.
finetuned: The worship of the senses has always been blamed, because men instinctively dread passions and sensations which are more potent than themselves, and which are common to them with the lower animals. But Dorian Gray thought that the real soul of the senses had not been discovered. He thought that they had remained savage and animal because society had tried to repress or destroy them instead of fostering them as parts of a new religion in which beauty was the object. Looking back upon the history of the race, he felt a deep sense of loss. So much had been sacrificed for so little gain, and the extreme abhorrence of pleasure had been the result of fear, and the painful renunciation of the self had been the punishment of an evil which was far worse than the imagined evil which they had set out to avoid. Nature, in her irony, drove the ascetic into the wilds and gave him beasts for companions instead of men.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
input:
"Your life seems quite troubling, full of challenges that may have led you down a difficult path. It appears that your journey has culminated in some serious decisions. As I consider my next steps, it’s not your life that occupies my thoughts."

"Ah, Alan," Dorian replied softly with a sigh, "I wish you could feel even a small fraction of the compassion for me that I feel for you." He then turned his gaze toward the garden. Campbell remained silent in response.
human:
“Your life? Good heavens! what a life that is! You have gone from corruption to corruption, and now you have culminated in crime. In doing what I am going to do - what you force me to do - it is not of your life that I am thinking.”

“Ah, Alan,” murmured Dorian with a sigh, “I wish you had a thousandth part of the pity for me that I have for you.” He turned away as he spoke and stood looking out at the garden. Campbell made no answer.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
input:
When a highly respected physician, who also happens to be one's husband, tells friends and family that there is likely nothing wrong except for a temporary bout of nervous depression and a minor tendency toward hysteria, it leaves one in a difficult position. 

My brother, who is also a physician of similar reputation, shares the same opinion.

As a result, I am advised to take phosphates or phosphites—whichever it may be—along with tonics, travel, fresh air, and exercise, while being strongly discouraged from engaging in any work until I feel better. In summary, the situation involves navigating the recommendations of trusted medical professionals while managing personal health concerns.

My brother is also a physician, and also of high standing, and he says the same thing.

So I take phosphates or phosphites - whichever it is, and tonics, and journeys, and air, and exercise, and am absolutely forbidden to “work” until I am well again.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
input:
It is rare for ordinary individuals such as John and me to acquire ancestral homes for the summer. 

A colonial mansion, a hereditary estate, or even a haunted house would be a delightful notion, yet that may be too much to hope for. 

If it were not, why would it be rented at such a low price? Additionally, why has it remained unoccupied for so long? 

John is exceedingly practical. He lacks patience for faith, harbors a strong aversion to superstition, and openly mocks any discussions of concepts that cannot be experienced through the senses or quantified.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
input:
John has never seemed nervous in his life. He finds amusement in my reaction to the wallpaper. 

Initially, he planned to replace it, but later he suggested that I was allowing it to dominate my thoughts. He asserted that for someone with a nervous disposition, indulging such whims is detrimental.

He explained that if the wallpaper were removed, I would then focus on the heavy bedstead, followed by the barred windows, and ultimately the gate at the top of the stairs, and so forth.
human:
I suppose John never was nervous in his life. He laughs at me so about this wallpaper!

At first he meant to repaper the room, but afterwards he said that I was letting it get the better of me, and that nothing was worse for a nervous patient than to give way to such fancies.

He said that after the wallpaper was changed it would be the heavy bedstead, and then the barred windows, and then that gate at the head of the stairs, and so on.

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input: As we prepared to sign the aforementioned articles, which would bind us and our heirs for fifty years, Mr. Brockden, the scrivener, addressed us. He noted, "You are young men, but it is unlikely that any of you will live to see the end of the term established in the document." Despite his assertion, several of us are still living today. However, the instrument was rendered void just a few years later due to a charter that incorporated the company and granted it perpetual status.

A number of us, however, are yet living; but the instrument was after a few years rendered null by a charter that incorporated and gave perpetuity to the company.

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input: Mr. Logan, who adhered to the Quaker faith, wrote an address in support of defensive war, providing several strong arguments for his stance. He entrusted me with sixty pounds to be invested in lottery tickets for the battery, with instructions for any prizes to be dedicated solely to that purpose. He shared an anecdote about his former employer, William Penn, regarding the topic of defense. As a young man, Penn traveled from England with his proprietary and served as their secretary during a time of war. Their ship was pursued by an armed vessel believed to be an enemy. The captain prepared for defense but informed Penn and the Quakers that their assistance was not anticipated, encouraging them to retreat to the cabin. However, James Logan chose to remain on deck and took his position by a gun. Ultimately, the supposed enemy turned out to be an ally, and no conflict ensued. When Logan returned below deck to share this information, Penn reprimanded him for remaining on deck and participating in defense, citing the principles of Friends and that such action had not been requested by the captain. This rebuke, delivered in front of others, irritated Logan, who responded, "As your servant, why did you not command me to come down? It seemed you were content for me to help defend the ship when you perceived danger."
human: The honorable and learned Mr. Logan, who had always been of that sect, was one who wrote an address to them, declaring his approbation of defensive war, and supporting his opinion by many strong arguments. He put into my hands sixty pounds to be laid out in lottery tickets for the battery, with directions to apply what prizes might be drawn wholly to that service. He told me the following anecdote of his old master, William Penn, respecting defense. He came over from England, when a young man, with that proprietary, and as his secretary. It was war-time, and their ship was chas'd by an armed vessel, suppos'd to be an enemy. Their captain prepar'd for defense; but told William Penn, and his company of Quakers, that he did not expect their assistance, and they might retire into the cabin, which they did, except James Logan, who chose to stay upon deck, and was quarter'd to a gun. The suppos'd enemy prov'd a friend, so there was no fighting; but when the secretary went down to communicate the intelligence, William Penn rebuk'd him severely for staying upon deck, and undertaking to assist in defending the vessel, contrary to the principles of Friends, especially as it had not been required by the captain. This reproof, being before all the company, piqu'd the secretary, who answer'd, "I being thy servant, why did thee not order me to come down? But thee was willing enough that I should stay and help to fight the ship when thee thought there was danger."

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input: I stayed there for nearly three months, and by that time I could count among my new friends Judge Allen, Samuel Bustill, the secretary of the Province, Isaac Pearson, Joseph Cooper, and several members of the Smith family who were in the Assembly, as well as Isaac Decow, the surveyor-general. The latter was a shrewd and wise old man who told me that he had started out on his own when he was young by hauling clay for brick-makers, learned to write after he had reached adulthood, carried the chain for surveyors who then taught him surveying, and had now, through his own hard work, acquired a comfortable estate. He said to me, "I foresee that you will soon take this man's business away from him and make a fortune in it at Philadelphia." At that time he had no idea at all that I intended to set up there or anywhere else. These friends were later very helpful to me, just as I was occasionally helpful to some of them, and they all continued to think well of me for as long as they lived.

title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
input:
A journey to New England was undertaken this year due to post-office business, during which the College of Cambridge conferred upon me the degree of Master of Arts. This highlights the fact that I received this honor without having studied at any college. Previously, Yale College in Connecticut had also awarded me a similar degree, in recognition of my contributions to the field of electricity in natural philosophy. 

The prospect of war with France in 1754 led to the organization of a congress of commissioners from various colonies, as ordered by the Lords of Trade. This congress was to assemble at Albany to discuss defense strategies with the chiefs of the Six Nations, aiming to protect both their territory and ours. Governor Hamilton informed the House of this development and requested that they provide suitable gifts for the Indian leaders. He also nominated the speaker, Mr. Norris, and myself, along with Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters, to serve as commissioners for Pennsylvania. The House approved these nominations and supplied the necessary goods for the gifts, although they were not entirely enthusiastic about conducting negotiations outside of the province. Ultimately, we met with the other commissioners at Albany in mid-June. This suggests that the colonies were taking steps to coordinate their efforts and build alliances in preparation for potential conflict.

They were conferr'd in consideration of my improvements and discoveries in the electric branch of natural philosophy.

Governor Hamilton, having receiv'd this order, acquainted the House with it, requesting they would furnish proper presents for the Indians, to be given on this occasion; and naming the speaker (Mr. Norris) and myself to join Mr. Thomas Penn and Mr. Secretary Peters as commissioners to act for Pennsylvania. The House approv'd the nomination, and provided the goods for the present, and tho' they did not much like treating out of the provinces; and we met the other commissioners at Albany about the middle of June.

title: Walden
input: Additionally, it appears that certain individuals perceive the entirety of human existence as having been thoroughly explored by their predecessors, with all aspects of life, including both the most elevated and the most mundane, having been carefully considered. Furthermore, according to Evelyn, historical figures such as Solomon and the Roman prætors have established guidelines for various aspects of life, including the placement of trees and the frequency with which one may enter a neighbor's property to collect items that have fallen onto it. Moreover, prominent figures like Hippocrates have even provided instructions on seemingly trivial matters, such as the proper method for cutting one's nails, which, in this case, is to trim them to a length that is even with the tips of the fingers. In essence, the feelings of tedium and ennui that arenote to have exhausted the diversity and pleasures of life are, in fact, as ancient as humanity itself. It is worth noting that human capabilities have never been fully assessed, and it is unwise to evaluate an individual's potential based on past achievements, given that so little has been attempted. Moreover, regardless of any past failures, it is advisable not to be disheartened, for it is impossible to determine what tasks remain unaccomplished, and thus, one should not be unduly troubled by unfulfilled potential.
human: The whole ground of human life seems to some to have been gone over by their predecessors, both the heights and the valleys, and all things to have been cared for. According to Evelyn, “the wise Solomon prescribed ordinances for the very distances of trees; and the Roman prætors have decided how often you may go into your neighbor’s land to gather the acorns which fall on it without trespass, and what share belongs to that neighbor.” Hippocrates has even left directions how we should cut our nails; that is, even with the ends of the fingers, neither shorter nor longer. Undoubtedly the very tedium and ennui which presume to have exhausted the variety and the joys of life are as old as Adam. But man’s capacities have never been measured; nor are we to judge of what he can do by any precedents, so little has been tried. Whatever have been thy failures hitherto, “be not afflicted, my child, for who shall assign to thee what thou hast left undone?”

Evelyn says that historical figures like Solomon and the Roman prætors have set rules for many things, like where to plant trees and how often you can go onto a neighbor’s land to pick up things that fell there. Even Hippocrates gave advice on small things, such as how to cut your nails—trim them so they’re even with the tips of your fingers. In fact, the feeling of boredom and tiredness that says there’s nothing left to experience is as old as humans themselves. It’s important to remember that human abilities have never been completely measured, and it’s not wise to judge someone’s future based on what they’ve done before, since so little has been tried. Also, no matter past mistakes, don’t be discouraged, because we can’t know what’s still left to do. So don’t worry too much about what you haven’t achieved.

Solomon and the Roman prætors have prescribed the places where trees may be planted, and how often you may go to your neighbour’s to pick up what has fallen on his ground. Hippocrates has even prescribed how you must cut your nails, and that is, you must cut them to the very tips of the fingers. The feelings of weariness and ennui which are not sufficient to exhaust the variety and pleasures of life are as old as man himself. Human powers have never been measured, and it is unwise to measure a man’s capacity by his past achievements, so little has been done. Whether he may have failed before, let him not be disheartened, for it is impossible to know what has not been done, and therefore let him not be unduly concerned about unfulfilled powers.

title: Walden
input: It is worth noting that my extensive engagement with beans constituted a unique experience, encompassing the processes of planting, hoeing, harvesting, threshing, and ultimately selling them; the latter task proved to be the most challenging of all, although I may add that tasting the beans also formed a part of my endeavor. My resolve to understand beans was unwavering. During their growth, I would hoe from five o’clock in the morning until noon and typically spent the remainder of the day attending to other responsibilities. Furthermore, one must consider the profound and intricate familiarity one develops with various types of weeds; this aspect merits some elaboration, as the labor involved was certainly repetitive. I ruthlessly disrupted their delicate structures, making stark distinctions with my hoe, leveling entire rows of one species while meticulously cultivating another. That is Roman wormwood; that is pigweed; that is sorrel; that is piper-grass—one must engage with them, sever their roots from the earth, exposing them to the sun, as any remaining fiber in the shade enables them to revert, becoming as verdant as a leek within two days. It was a prolonged struggle, not against cranes but rather against weeds, those persistent adversaries that enjoyed the advantages of sun, rain, and dew. Daily, the beans witnessed my arrival as I came to their defense, armed with a hoe, systematically thinning the ranks of their foes and filling the trenches with the fallen weeds. Many a formidable Hector, towering a full foot above his fellow competitors, succumbed to my efforts and lay defeated in the dust.
human: It was a singular experience that long acquaintance which I cultivated with beans, what with planting, and hoeing, and harvesting, and threshing, and picking over and selling them, - the last was the hardest of all, - I might add eating, for I did taste. I was determined to know beans. When they were growing, I used to hoe from five o’clock in the morning till noon, and commonly spent the rest of the day about other affairs. Consider the intimate and curious acquaintance one makes with various kinds of weeds, - it will bear some iteration in the account, for there was no little iteration in the labor, - disturbing their delicate organizations so ruthlessly, and making such invidious distinctions with his hoe, levelling whole ranks of one species, and sedulously cultivating another. That’s Roman wormwood, - that’s pigweed, - that’s sorrel, - that’s piper-grass, - have at him, chop him up, turn his roots upward to the sun, don’t let him have a fibre in the shade, if you do he’ll turn himself t’other side up and be as green as a leek in two days. A long war, not with cranes, but with weeds, those Trojans who had sun and rain and dews on their side. Daily the beans saw me come to their rescue armed with a hoe, and thin the ranks of their enemies, filling up the trenches with weedy dead. Many a lusty crest-waving Hector, that towered a whole foot above his crowding comrades, fell before my weapon and rolled in the dust.
base: My time with beans was unique. I planted, hoes, harvested, threshed, and sold them. Selling was the hardest part, though I should mention I also tasted the beans. I was determined to understand beans. While they grew, I hoes from five in the morning until noon, then did other things. Weeds became familiar, and that’s something to note. The work was repetitive. I destroyed their roots, exposing them to the sun. Any left in the shade would grow again, like a leek in two days. It was a long fight, not against cranes but weeds. They had sun, rain, dew. Every day, I came to help the beans, using a hoe to thin the weeds. Many big weeds, a foot taller, fell and lay in the dust.
finetuned: It was a strange experience, however, my long acquaintance with the beans, - planting, hoeing, harvesting, threshing, and selling them; the last was the hardest of all, and I may say tasting the beans was part of the business. I was determined to know beans. When they were growing I would hoe from five o’clock in the morning till noon, and then I generally went to work some more. One must consider how thoroughly one becomes familiar with different weeds; it is a subject worthy of some consideration, for the work was certainly monotonous. I broke their delicate structures with ruthless violence, making a clean division with my hoe, and levelled whole rows of one kind while cultivating another with great care. That is Roman wormwood; that is pigweed; that is sorrel; that is piper-grass; - you must deal with them, tear out their roots from the earth, and let them lie in the sun, for if there is any fibre in the shade they will recover, and in two days be as green as a leek. It was a long struggle, not against cranes, but against weeds, those persistent foes, with whom the sun, the rain, and the dew had been on good terms. Every day the beans saw me come to their defence, armed with a hoe, thinning their ranks, and filling the trenches with the fallen weeds. Many a mighty Hector, a full foot higher than his fellow-contestants, fell beneath my hand, and lay down defeated in the dust.

title: Walden
input:
At midnight, when the moon was present, I would occasionally encounter hounds in my path as I walked through the woods. These animals would retreat from my way, seemingly fearful, and remain silent among the bushes until I had passed by. Meanwhile, squirrels and wild mice would compete for the store of nuts that I had accumulated. 

The area surrounding my house featured numerous pitch-pines, ranging in diameter from one to four inches, which had been damaged by mice during the previous winter. The winter had been particularly harsh for these animals, with deep snow covering the ground for an extended period, forcing them to incorporate a significant amount of pine bark into their diet. Nevertheless, by mid-summer, these trees appeared to be alive and thriving, with many of them having grown approximately one foot, despite being completely girdled. However, after enduring another winter, the girdled trees were invariably dead. It is noteworthy that a single mouse is able to consume an entire pine tree, gnawing around the trunk rather than up and down, and this phenomenon may be necessary to regulate the density of these trees, which tend to grow in close proximity to one another.
human:
At midnight, when there was a moon, I sometimes met with hounds in my path prowling about the woods, which would skulk out of my way, as if afraid, and stand silent amid the bushes till I had passed.

Squirrels and wild mice disputed for my store of nuts. There were scores of pitch-pines around my house, from one to four inches in diameter, which had been gnawed by mice the previous winter, - a Norwegian winter for them, for the snow lay long and deep, and they were obliged to mix a large proportion of pine bark with their other diet. These trees were alive and apparently flourishing at mid-summer, and many of them had grown a foot, though completely girdled; but after another winter such were without exception dead. It is remarkable that a single mouse should thus be allowed a whole pine tree for its dinner, gnawing round instead of up and down it; but perhaps it is necessary in order to thin these trees, which are wont to grow up densely.

But by summer, the trees looked alive, some even grew a foot. Yet after another winter, the girdled ones were dead. A mouse can eat a whole tree, chewing around the trunk, not up and down. Maybe that helps keep the trees from getting too close to each other.

title: Walden
input: I observe the flow of morning cars with a sense of familiarity similar to that of watching the sun rise, which can often feel just as predictable. The trails of clouds stretching behind and ascending higher may briefly obscure the sun, casting my distant field into shadow, while the cars make their way to Boston. This celestial display can seem to diminish the significance of the earthly train of cars. The caretaker of the locomotive was up early on this winter morning, illuminated by starlight in the mountains, attending to his duties. Fire was stirred awake at this early hour to provide the necessary warmth and prepare the engine for its journey. If only the endeavor were as innocent as it is timely! When snow covers the ground, they may equip the engine with snow shoes and utilize a powerful plow to clear a path from the mountains to the coast, through which the cars, like a trailing drill, distribute restless passengers and goods across the nation. Throughout the day, the locomotive travels over the landscape, pausing only to allow its operator a rest. I sometimes find myself awakened at midnight by the engine’s heavy footsteps and forceful snorts, as it faces the harsh elements in a secluded forest, and it may only return to its station with the morning star, ready to embark on another journey without pause. Alternatively, I might hear it in the evening, releasing excess energy in its stable to relax before a few hours of rest. If only this endeavor were as noble and commanding as it is relentless and tireless!
human: I watch the passage of the morning cars with the same feeling that I do the rising of the sun, which is hardly more regular. Their train of clouds stretching far behind and rising higher and higher, going to heaven while the cars are going to Boston, conceals the sun for a minute and casts my distant field into the shade, a celestial train beside which the petty train of cars which hugs the earth is but the barb of the spear. The stabler of the iron horse was up early this winter morning by the light of the stars amid the mountains, to fodder and harness his steed. Fire, too, was awakened thus early to put the vital heat in him and get him off. If the enterprise were as innocent as it is early! If the snow lies deep, they strap on his snow-shoes, and with the giant plow, plow a furrow from the mountains to the seaboard, in which the cars, like a following drill-barrow, sprinkle all the restless men and floating merchandise in the country for seed. All day the fire-steed flies over the country, stopping only that his master may rest, and I am awakened by his tramp and defiant snort at midnight, when in some remote glen in the woods he fronts the elements incased in ice and snow; and he will reach his stall only with the morning star, to start once more on his travels without rest or slumber. Or perchance, at evening, I hear him in his stable blowing off the superfluous energy of the day, that he may calm his nerves and cool his liver and brain for a few hours of iron slumber. If the enterprise were as heroic and commanding as it is protracted and unwearied!

The clouds trail behind, rising higher, sometimes blocking the sun for a moment, casting my field into shadow while the cars head toward Boston. This sky scene makes the cars seem less important. The train conductor was up early on this winter morning, lit by mountain stars, doing his job. Fire was lit to keep warm and ready the engine for its trip. If only this work were as simple as it is timely! When snow is on the ground, they put on snow shoes and use a big plow to clear a path from the mountains to the coast, where the cars, like a trailing drill, carry people and things across the country. All day, the engine moves over the land, stopping only to let the driver rest. I sometimes wake up at midnight to the engine’s heavy steps and loud noises as it faces the cold in a forest, and it returns to its station with the morning star, ready for another trip. Or I might hear it in the evening, letting out energy in its stable before a few hours of sleep. If only this work were as noble as it is hard and never stopping!

The man who tended the locomotive was up early on this wintry morning, starlight in the mountains, tending his business. Fire was stoked awake at this early hour to warm and prepare the engine for the journey. If only the enterprise were as innocent as it is timely! When the snow falls, they put on snow-shoes to the engine, and use a powerful plow to make a passage from the mountains to the coast, through which the cars, like a trailing drill, distribute restless passengers and goods over the country. All day long the locomotive drives over the landscape, only stopping to let the operator rest. I am sometimes awakened at midnight by the engine’s heavy footsteps and roaring snorts, as it faces the elements in a secluded forest, and it only returns to its station with the morning star, ready for another journey without a pause. Or I hear it in the evening, blowing off its excess in the stable to get to sleep before a few hours’ rest. If only the enterprise were as noble and commanding as it is relentless and tireless!

title: Walden
input: The indescribable innocence and benevolence of Nature, encompassing the sun, wind, and rain, as well as the seasons of summer and winter, provide an enduring sense of health and joy. Additionally, the deep connection that exists between Nature and humanity is so profound that, were any individual to experience genuine sorrow for justifiable reasons, the entirety of Nature would respond accordingly: the brightness of the sun would diminish, the winds would express a humane sigh, the clouds would weep, and the trees would shed their leaves, donning a veil of mourning even in the height of summer. It is worth noting that I seek to engage in a dialogue with the earth, pondering whether I am not, in part, composed of leaves and the very essence of the soil.
human: The indescribable innocence and beneficence of Nature, - of sun and wind and rain, of summer and winter, - such health, such cheer, they afford forever! and such sympathy have they ever with our race, that all Nature would be affected, and the sun’s brightness fade, and the winds would sigh humanely, and the clouds rain tears, and the woods shed their leaves and put on mourning in midsummer, if any man should ever for a just cause grieve. Shall I not have intelligence with the earth? Am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself?
base: Nature’s innocent and kind spirit, with the sun, wind, and rain, and the changing seasons of summer and winter, brings a lasting feeling of health and happiness. There is a deep bond between Nature and people so strong that if someone truly felt sad for a good reason, all of Nature would react: the sun would grow dimmer, the winds would sigh gently, the clouds would weep, and the trees would drop their leaves, wearing a veil of sorrow even in the middle of summer. I wonder if I, too, am made of leaves and the very heart of the earth, and if I am speaking to the ground in a way that matters.
finetuned: The inexpressible innocence and goodness of Nature, of the sun and wind and rain, of summer and winter, give a perpetual health and happiness. The tie between Nature and man is so close that if any man were truly sad for some reason, the whole of Nature would be sad: the brightness of the sun would be lessened, the winds would breathe a human sigh, the clouds would weep, the trees would shed their leaves, and wear a veil of mourning even in summer. I wish to talk with the earth and ask whether I am not partly of leaves and of the very heart of the soil.

title: Heart of Darkness
input:
The manager positioned himself beside the wheel, murmuring confidentially about the imperative of navigating well down the river before nightfall. It was at this moment that I observed a clearing in the distance along the riverside, accompanied by the outlines of what appeared to be a building. "What is this?" I inquired. He clapped his hands in amazement and exclaimed, "The station!" I immediately maneuvered the vessel closer while maintaining a cautious speed. 

Through my binoculars, I discerned the slope of a hill dotted with sparse trees, entirely devoid of undergrowth. A long, deteriorating structure atop the hill was partially obscured by tall grass; the expansive gaps in the peaked roof appeared dark from a distance. The surrounding jungle and woods formed a striking backdrop. There was an absence of any enclosure or fencing; however, it was evident that one had once existed, as I noted half a dozen slender posts remaining in a row near the house, each crudely trimmed and adorned with rounded carved balls at their upper ends. The rails or similar barriers that had previously connected them had vanished, enveloped by the encroaching forest. The riverbank remained clear, revealing a white man beneath a hat resembling a cart-wheel who was gesturing insistently with his entire arm. Upon scrutinizing the edges of the forest both above and below, I became increasingly convinced that I could perceive movements—human figures gliding discreetly to and fro. I proceeded past with caution, subsequently halting the engines to allow the vessel to drift downstream. The man on the shore began to call out, urging us to dock. "We have been attacked," the manager shouted in alarm. "I know—I know. It is all right," the other responded, his tone remarkably cheerful. "Come along. It is all right. I am glad."
human:
“The manager stood by the wheel murmuring confidentially about the necessity of getting well away down the river before dark at all events, when I saw in the distance a clearing on the riverside and the outlines of some sort of building. ‘What’s this?’ I asked. He clapped his hands in wonder. ‘The station!’ he cried. I edged in at once, still going half-speed.

“Through my glasses I saw the slope of a hill interspersed with rare trees and perfectly free from undergrowth. A long decaying building on the summit was half buried in the high grass; the large holes in the peaked roof gaped black from afar; the jungle and the woods made a background. There was no enclosure or fence of any kind; but there had been one apparently, for near the house half-a-dozen slim posts remained in a row, roughly trimmed, and with their upper ends ornamented with round carved balls. The rails, or whatever there had been between, had disappeared. Of course the forest surrounded all that. The river-bank was clear, and on the waterside I saw a white man under a hat like a cart-wheel beckoning persistently with his whole arm. Examining the edge of the forest above and below, I was almost certain I could see movements - human forms gliding here and there. I steamed past prudently, then stopped the engines and let her drift down. The man on the shore began to shout, urging us to land. ‘We have been attacked,’ screamed the manager. ‘I know - I know. It’s all right,’ yelled back the other, as cheerful as you please. ‘Come along. It’s all right. I am glad.’
base: The manager stood next to the wheel, whispering about the need to get down the river before dark. I saw a clearing ahead along the riverbank, with shapes that looked like a building. "What is that?" I asked. He slapped his hands and said, "The station!" I brought the boat closer, moving slowly. With binoculars, I saw a hill with trees, no underbrush. A broken building on top of the hill was hidden by tall grass. The roof had big gaps, looking dark from far away. The jungle and woods around it were sharp against the background. There was no fence or enclosure, but I saw six posts in a line near the house, cut short and with rounded balls on top. The rails that once connected them were gone, swallowed by the forest. The riverbank was clear, showing a white man under a hat like a cart wheel, waving his arm. Looking around the forest, I saw people moving quietly. I went on carefully, then turned off the engine so the boat drifted down. The man on shore started shouting, telling us to come in. "We've been attacked," the manager said. "I know—I know. It's all right," the other said, sounding happy. "Come on. It's all right. I'm glad."
finetuned:
The manager stood beside the wheel, whispering confidentially about the necessity of passing well down the river before nightfall. It was here that I saw a clearing in the distance along the riverside, with the shadow of a building. “What is this?” I asked. He clapped his hands in astonishment, and exclaimed, “The station!” I immediately brought the vessel nearer, keeping to a cautious speed.

Through my binoculars I saw the slope of a hill covered with scattered trees, with no undergrowth. A long, dilapidated building upon the hill was half hidden by tall grass; the great spaces in the peaked roof seemed black at a distance. The jungle and woods formed a fine background. There was no enclosure or fence; but it was evident that one had once existed, as I noted half a dozen slender posts in a row near the house, each crudely trimmed and with rounded carved balls at the upper ends. The rails or like barriers that had connected them had disappeared, swallowed up by the advancing forest. The bank was clear, and a white man under a hat like a cart-wheel was pointing insistently with his whole arm. Looking at the edges of the forest both above and below, I grew more and more convinced that I could see movements - human figures gliding stealthily to and fro. I passed cautiously, and then stopped the engines to let the vessel drift down. The man on the shore began to shout at us to come in. “We’ve been attacked,” the manager shouted in alarm. “I know - I know. It’s all right,” the other answered, in a remarkably cheerful voice. “Come along. It’s all right. I’m glad.”

title: Heart of Darkness
input: His presence seemed to embody a profound darkness. I regarded him as one might observe someone at the bottom of a ravine where light rarely penetrates. However, my time to attend to him was limited, as I was assisting the engine driver in disassembling the leaking cylinders, straightening a bent connecting rod, and managing other similar tasks. My environment was often chaotic, filled with rust, metal shavings, nuts, bolts, wrenches, hammers, and ratchet drills—items I typically found challenging to work with. I looked after the small forge we were fortunate to have on board and labored diligently amidst what felt like a disorganized pile of scrap, unless my condition prevented me from standing. Overall, my efforts were focused on maintaining the machinery while navigating the difficulties of my surroundings.
human: “His was an impenetrable darkness. I looked at him as you peer down at a man who is lying at the bottom of a precipice where the sun never shines. But I had not much time to give him, because I was helping the engine-driver to take to pieces the leaky cylinders, to straighten a bent connecting-rod, and in other such matters. I lived in an infernal mess of rust, filings, nuts, bolts, spanners, hammers, ratchet-drills - things I abominate, because I don’t get on with them. I tended the little forge we fortunately had aboard; I toiled wearily in a wretched scrap-heap - unless I had the shakes too bad to stand.
base: His presence felt like a deep shadow. I saw him as someone at the bottom of a ravine where light doesn’t reach. But I couldn’t spend much time on him. I was helping the engine driver take apart leaking cylinders, fix a bent rod, and do other things like that. The place was always loud and messy, full of rust, metal bits, nuts, bolts, wrenches, hammers, and drills. Those things usually made me uneasy. I kept the small forge we had on the ship and worked hard in what felt like a heap of scrap, unless I was too sick to stand. Most of the time, I was just trying to keep the machines running while dealing with the mess around me.

But my time to give him any attention was short, for I was helping the engine-driver to take the leaking cylinders to pieces, to straighten a bent connecting-rod, and to do other things of the same kind. My surroundings were full of rust, and of metal shavings and nuts and bolts and wrenches and hammers and ratchet-drills - things that I did not care for. I looked after the little forge we had on board, and worked hard among what I considered a heap of rubbish, unless my condition prevented my standing.

title: Heart of Darkness
input: In essence, during my childhood, I harbored a profound fascination for maps. I would spend countless hours studying regions such as South America, Africa, and Australia, immersing myself in the wonders of exploration. At that time, there existed numerous blank spaces on the globe, and whenever I encountered a particularly enticing area on a map—though, in truth, all of them appeared inviting—I would place my finger on it and declare, “When I grow up, I shall travel there.” The North Pole was among these alluring destinations that I distinctly recall. However, I have yet to visit it and do not intend to pursue that aspiration now, as the allure has diminished. Furthermore, various other locations were scattered across the hemispheres. I have had the opportunity to visit some of those places, and the experiences are best left unexamined. Nevertheless, there remained one destination—the largest and most uncharted, so to speak—that I longed to explore.
human: “Now when I was a little chap I had a passion for maps. I would look for hours at South America, or Africa, or Australia, and lose myself in all the glories of exploration. At that time there were many blank spaces on the earth, and when I saw one that looked particularly inviting on a map (but they all look that) I would put my finger on it and say, ‘When I grow up I will go there.’ The North Pole was one of these places, I remember. Well, I haven’t been there yet, and shall not try now. The glamour’s off. Other places were scattered about the hemispheres. I have been in some of them, and... well, we won’t talk about that. But there was one yet - the biggest, the most blank, so to speak - that I had a hankering after.
base: When I was a kid, I loved maps a lot. I’d spend a lot of time looking at places like South America, Africa, and Australia, getting really into the idea of exploring. Back then, there were a lot of blank spots on the world map, and every time I saw a place that seemed cool—well, actually, every place did—my finger would go there and I’d say, “One day, I’m going to travel there.” The North Pole was one of those places I remembered clearly. But I never went there and don’t plan to anymore, because it doesn’t feel as exciting now. There were other places all over the world I got to visit, and those experiences are best left alone. But there was still one place—the biggest and most unknown one—that I always wanted to see.
finetuned: In my boyhood I was passionately fond of maps. I used to sit up all night studying South America, Africa, and Australia, and all the other wonderful places that one could find on the globe. There were so many blank spaces, and whenever I came upon any particularly interesting one, which, in fact, were all of them, I would lay my finger on it and say, “When I am grown up I will go there.” The North Pole was one of the most fascinating of the places that I remember. But I have never gone there, and I don’t intend to go there now, because the charm has gone out of it. There were other places scattered about the hemispheres, and I have gone to some of them, and you may leave them out. But there was one place left, the largest and most unexplored, as it were, that I longed to go to.

title: Heart of Darkness
input: She extended her arms as if reaching for a departing figure, stretching them back with her pale hands clasped against the dimming light of the window. It may seem unlikely, but I could see him quite clearly at that moment. It seems that this poignant image will remain with me for as long as I live, and I may also remember her—a tragic and familiar presence—who, in this gesture, resembles another sorrowful figure adorned with powerless allure, reaching bare brown arms over the shimmering darkness of the stream. Then, in a soft voice, she remarked, "He died as he lived." This scene captures a blend of loss and remembrance.
human: “She put out her arms as if after a retreating figure, stretching them back and with clasped pale hands across the fading and narrow sheen of the window. Never see him! I saw him clearly enough then. I shall see this eloquent phantom as long as I live, and I shall see her, too, a tragic and familiar Shade, resembling in this gesture another one, tragic also, and bedecked with powerless charms, stretching bare brown arms over the glitter of the infernal stream, the stream of darkness. She said suddenly very low, ‘He died as he lived.’
base: She stretched her arms out as if trying to catch a figure that was fading away, pulling them back with her pale hands pressed against the fading light from the window. I could see him clearly then, even though it might seem odd. That image will stay with me for the rest of my life, and I might also remember her—a tragic, familiar figure—who, in that moment, looked like another sad person with no real power, reaching out with bare brown arms over the shimmering dark of the stream. Then she whispered, "He died as he lived." This moment mixes loss with memory.
finetuned: She stretched out her arms as if to clutch at a departing figure, and stretched them back with her white hands against the fading light of the window. I could see him quite plainly then, for it seemed impossible. It seems that this touching picture will live in me as long as I live, and I may remember her - the tragic and familiar presence - who, in this gesture, is like another tragic figure girded with helpless charm, who stretches out bare brown arms over the rippling darkness of the stream. Then, in a low voice she said, "He died as he lived."

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: I consider my departure from Colonel Lloyd's plantation to be one of the most significant events in my life. It is possible, and indeed quite likely, that had I not been relocated from that plantation to Baltimore, I would today find myself, rather than seated at my own table experiencing freedom and the joys of home while composing this narrative, in the distressing confines of slavery. The move to Baltimore established the foundation and opened the door to all my future successes. I have consistently viewed this event as the initial clear indication of that kind providence which has continuously accompanied me and enriched my life with numerous blessings. Furthermore, I found the selection of myself to be rather remarkable. There were several other enslaved children who could have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore, including those who were younger, those who were older, and those who were of a similar age. Ultimately, I was chosen from among them all, being the first, last, and sole selection.
human: I look upon my departure from Colonel Lloyd’s plantation as one of the most interesting events of my life. It is possible, and even quite probable, that but for the mere circumstance of being removed from that plantation to Baltimore, I should have to-day, instead of being here seated by my own table, in the enjoyment of freedom and the happiness of home, writing this Narrative, been confined in the galling chains of slavery. Going to live at Baltimore laid the foundation, and opened the gateway, to all my subsequent prosperity. I have ever regarded it as the first plain manifestation of that kind providence which has ever since attended me, and marked my life with so many favors. I regarded the selection of myself as being somewhat remarkable. There were a number of slave children that might have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore. There were those younger, those older, and those of the same age. I was chosen from among them all, and was the first, last, and only choice.
base: Leaving Colonel Lloyd's plantation was one of the most important things that ever happened to me. It's probably true that if I hadn't been sent from that place to Baltimore, I would still be in slavery, suffering in the dark and cramped quarters, instead of sitting at my own table, free and happy, writing this story. Moving to Baltimore was the start of everything else that came after. I've always seen this as the first sign that something good was happening to me, that God was watching over me and giving me many good things. Also, being chosen was special. There were other enslaved children who could have gone to Baltimore, some younger, some older, some the same age as me. But I was the one chosen, the first, the last, the only one.
finetuned: I count my leaving Colonel Lloyd’s plantation one of the greatest events in my life. Had I not been taken from that plantation to Baltimore, I should to-day, instead of sitting at my own table enjoying freedom and the pleasures of home while writing this history, be in the wretched dungeon of slavery. The removal to Baltimore was the beginning and opened the door to all my future success. I have always regarded this event as the first clear indication of that kind providence which has ever attended me and blessed my life with so many favors. I found the choice of myself very remarkable. There were several other slave children who could have been sent from the plantation to Baltimore, some younger than myself, some older, and some of my own age. I was chosen from among them all, the first and the last and the only one.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: Colonel Lloyd's home plantation resembled a small country village, serving as the center for various mechanical operations for multiple farms. Tasks such as shoemaking, blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain grinding were all carried out by the enslaved individuals on this plantation. This environment had a distinctly business-like atmosphere, setting it apart from the neighboring farms. The plantation featured numerous houses, further enhancing its significance compared to others in the area. Known among the enslaved as the Great House Farm, being chosen to run errands there was highly valued by those on the outlying farms. This association with prestige elevated its status in their minds. A slave selected for errands at the Great House Farm felt a sense of pride comparable to a politician elected to the American Congress, as it represented the overseers' trust in them. This privilege was sought not only for the esteem it brought but also as an escape from the harsh conditions of fieldwork. The individual who received this honor frequently was regarded as the most capable and reliable, and competitors for this position worked hard to gain favor from their overseers, similar to how political candidates seek to win over the electorate. Such dynamics reveal parallels between the behavior of Colonel Lloyd's enslaved individuals and those involved in political life.
human: The home plantation of Colonel Lloyd wore the appearance of a country village. All the mechanical operations for all the farms were performed here. The shoemaking and mending, the blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain-grinding, were all performed by the slaves on the home plantation. The whole place wore a business-like aspect very unlike the neighboring farms. The number of houses, too, conspired to give it advantage over the neighboring farms. It was called by the slaves the Great House Farm. Few privileges were esteemed higher, by the slaves of the out-farms, than that of being selected to do errands at the Great House Farm. It was associated in their minds with greatness. A representative could not be prouder of his election to a seat in the American Congress, than a slave on one of the out-farms would be of his election to do errands at the Great House Farm. They regarded it as evidence of great confidence reposed in them by their overseers; and it was on this account, as well as a constant desire to be out of the field from under the driver’s lash, that they esteemed it a high privilege, one worth careful living for. He was called the smartest and most trusty fellow, who had this honor conferred upon him the most frequently. The competitors for this office sought as diligently to please their overseers, as the office-seekers in the political parties seek to please and deceive the people. The same traits of character might be seen in Colonel Lloyd’s slaves, as are seen in the slaves of the political parties.
base: Colonel Lloyd's home plantation looked like a small country village. It was the main place where several farms did their work. Enslaved people made shoes, fixed metal, built carts, made barrels, wove cloth, and ground grain there. The place felt like a business, different from the other farms. There were a lot of houses, making it stand out. The enslaved called it the Great House Farm. Being sent there was a big deal. It was like being chosen for a important job. People on the other farms wanted to be chosen because it meant they were trusted. It was a way to feel important and get away from hard labor. The person chosen was usually the best and most dependable. Others worked hard to be liked by the overseers, just like politicians try to win votes. This shows how the enslaved acted like people in politics.
finetuned: Colonel Lloyd’s home plantation was a little country village, the centre of many mechanical operations for several farms. Shoemaking, blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain grinding, were all done by the slaves on this plantation. It had a business-like look, unlike the other farms. There were many houses there, more than in any other. It was called among the slaves the Great House Farm, and to be chosen to run errands there was the highest honor a slave could receive. He felt as much pride in it as a politician feels in being elected to the American Congress. It was a privilege sought for not only in the desire for honor, but also as an escape from the hardships of field labor. The man who received it was generally considered the best and most reliable, and all who sought the honor worked hard to gain the good-will of their overseers, as do all political candidates for the favor of the people.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: Additionally, I resided with Mr. Covey for a period of one year. Furthermore, during the initial six months of that year, it is worth noting that scarcely a week elapsed without his subjecting me to corporal punishment. In essence, I was rarely devoid of physical discomfort, as a sore back was a persistent affliction. Moreover, my lack of dexterity and coordination was frequently cited by Mr. Covey as a justification for administering physical discipline. It is worth noting that our workload was maximized to the point of tolerability. Moreover, our daily routine commenced well before dawn, at which time we would attend to the needs of our horses and subsequently proceed to the field with our agricultural equipment. Additionally, Mr. Covey provided us with a sufficient quantity of food, albeit with limited time allocated for consumption. In many instances, our meals were rushed, with fewer than five minutes devoted to eating. Moreover, our workdays were often excessively long, frequently commencing at the earliest light of day and persisting until the last remnants of daylight had faded; and during periods of intense agricultural activity, such as the preservation of fodder, it was not uncommon for midnight to arrive while we were still engaged in our tasks, including the binding of harvested crops.
human: I lived with Mr. Covey one year. During the first six months, of that year, scarce a week passed without his whipping me. I was seldom free from a sore back. My awkwardness was almost always his excuse for whipping me. We were worked fully up to the point of endurance. Long before day we were up, our horses fed, and by the first approach of day we were off to the field with our hoes and ploughing teams. Mr. Covey gave us enough to eat, but scarce time to eat it. We were often less than five minutes taking our meals. We were often in the field from the first approach of day till its last lingering ray had left us; and at saving-fodder time, midnight often caught us in the field binding blades.
base: I lived with Mr. Covey for a year. In the first six months, hardly a week went by without him punishing me. I was often in pain, especially with a sore back. My lack of skill and balance was often used as an excuse for the beatings. Our work was pushed to the limit. We started work before dawn, taking care of the horses and then going to the fields with the farming tools. Mr. Covey gave us enough food, but not much time to eat. Meals were usually quick, less than five minutes. Workdays were long, starting at dawn and ending when the day was done. During busy times like storing feed, we worked until midnight, still doing things like tying crops.
finetuned: I lived with Mr. Covey a year. In the first six months of that year scarcely a week passed without his whipping me. I was seldom without a sore back, and I was always at fault in my dexterity and coordination, which was his excuse for whipping me. Our work was pushed to the point of being endured. We rose before daybreak, attended to our horses, and went to the field with our farming outfit. Mr. Covey gave us a sufficient quantity of food, but not enough time to eat it; we were hurried to our meals, and had less than five minutes for eating. Our work-days were too long, often beginning at the earliest light and continuing till the last rays of daylight had passed away; and in the time of the preservation of fodder we were not unfrequently called at midnight still in the act of binding the cut corn.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
input: This mode of treatment exemplifies the broader system of deception and cruelty associated with slavery. It highlights how the approach taken seeks to instill a revulsion toward freedom by exposing the enslaved individuals only to its negative aspects. A notable example is when a slave, who has a fondness for molasses, steals some. In many instances, the master then goes to town and purchases a large quantity. Upon returning, the master forces the slave to consume the molasses until he becomes sickened by it. This method is similarly applied to discourage slaves from requesting more food than their standard allowance. When a slave exhausts his ration and seeks additional food, the master often reacts with anger but, rather than sending the slave away hungry, provides an excessive amount and mandates consumption within a specific timeframe. If the slave then expresses difficulty in eating the food, he may be punished for being discontented, as he is deemed neither satisfied nor fasting. This suggests a broader pattern of punitive measures aimed at controlling the desires and actions of enslaved individuals. The examples provided illustrate a prevalent practice within this system.
human: I have said that this mode of treatment is a part of the whole system of fraud and inhumanity of slavery. It is so. The mode here adopted to disgust the slave with freedom, by allowing him to see only the abuse of it, is carried out in other things. For instance, a slave loves molasses; he steals some. His master, in many cases, goes off to town, and buys a large quantity; he returns, takes his whip, and commands the slave to eat the molasses, until the poor fellow is made sick at the very mention of it. The same mode is sometimes adopted to make the slaves refrain from asking for more food than their regular allowance. A slave runs through his allowance, and applies for more. His master is enraged at him; but, not willing to send him off without food, gives him more than is necessary, and compels him to eat it within a given time. Then, if he complains that he cannot eat it, he is said to be satisfied neither full nor fasting, and is whipped for being hard to please! I have an abundance of such illustrations of the same principle, drawn from my own observation, but think the cases I have cited sufficient. The practice is a very common one.
base: This treatment shows the bigger picture of deception and cruelty in slavery. It shows how the method is meant to make people hate freedom by only showing them its bad sides. A good example is when a slave likes molasses and steals some. The master might go to town and buy a lot. Then the master makes the slave eat all of it until he feels sick. This same idea is used to stop slaves from asking for more food. If a slave runs out of his daily food and asks for more, the master gets angry but doesn’t send him away. Instead, he gives him a lot more and makes him eat it fast. If the slave says he can’t eat it, he gets punished for being unhappy. This shows a pattern of using punishment to control what enslaved people want and do. These examples show a common practice in this system.
finetuned: This treatment is the counterpart of the whole system of deception and cruelty connected with slavery. It is the attempt to instill a hatred of freedom by exhibiting the slaves only to its worst features. A slave who is fond of molasses steals some. The master goes to town, buys a large quantity, and on his return forces the slave to eat it until he is sick of it. The same plan is pursued in order to deter the slaves from asking for more food than their allowance. When a slave has consumed his ration and asks for more, the master is angry, but, instead of sending him away hungry, sends him to town and brings him back with a large quantity, and requires him to eat it in a certain time. If the slave then complains of not liking the food, he is whipped for being discontented, as he is neither satisfied nor fasting.

title: A Study in Scarlet
input: The reader may consider me a hopeless busybody when I admit how much this man stimulated my curiosity and how often I tried to break through the reticence he showed concerning himself. Before passing judgment, however, one should remember how aimless my life was and how little there was to occupy my attention. My health prevented me from going out unless the weather was exceptionally mild, and I had no friends who would visit me and interrupt the monotony of my daily existence. Under these circumstances, I eagerly welcomed the small mystery surrounding my companion and spent much of my time attempting to unravel it.

I spent a lot of time trying to solve it.

title: A Study in Scarlet
input: Jefferson Hope suggested that it may be advisable to start immediately, speaking in a calm yet determined tone that indicated his awareness of the serious danger they faced. He noted that while the front and back entrances are being monitored, it might be possible to escape through the side window and navigate across the fields with care. Once they reach the road, it is likely that they would only be a couple of miles from the Ravine where the horses are waiting. By daybreak, they could potentially be halfway through the mountains. Overall, the plan seems feasible if they proceed cautiously.
human: “We must make our start at once,” said Jefferson Hope, speaking in a low but resolute voice, like one who realizes the greatness of the peril, but has steeled his heart to meet it. “The front and back entrances are watched, but with caution we may get away through the side window and across the fields. Once on the road we are only two miles from the Ravine where the horses are waiting. By daybreak we should be half-way through the mountains.”

I reckon when we get to the road we’ll be no more than a couple of miles from the Ravine where the horses are waiting. By daylight we’ll be halfway up the mountains. I reckon it’ll work out all right if we don’t make too much noise.”

title: The Scarlet Letter
input: With the stigma lifted, Hester experienced a profound release, as the burdens of shame and anguish lifted from her spirit. This highlights the significant relief she felt, which she had not fully recognized until she experienced the freedom. Following this impulse, she removed the formal cap that had restricted her hair, allowing it to cascade over her shoulders, rich and dark, creating a contrast of shadow and light that softened her features. A radiant and tender smile emerged around her mouth and shone in her eyes, suggesting a deep connection to her femininity. A vibrant blush returned to her cheeks, which had long been pale. The aspects of her identity, including her youth and beauty, returned from what is often perceived as an irreversible past, merging with her youthful hope and an unfamiliar happiness in this moment. This signifies that the heaviness of the earth and sky dissipated alongside their sorrow. Suddenly, as if illuminated by a divine presence, sunlight broke through, flooding the previously shadowed forest, brightening each green leaf, transforming the yellow fallen leaves into gold, and illuminating the gray trunks of the trees. Objects that once cast shadows now embodied brightness. The path of the little brook could be traced by its joyful sparkle as it wound its way into the heart of the woods, which had transformed into a place of joy.
human: The stigma gone, Hester heaved a long, deep sigh, in which the burden of shame and anguish departed from her spirit. O exquisite relief! She had not known the weight, until she felt the freedom! By another impulse, she took off the formal cap that confined her hair; and down it fell upon her shoulders, dark and rich, with at once a shadow and a light in its abundance, and imparting the charm of softness to her features. There played around her mouth, and beamed out of her eyes, a radiant and tender smile, that seemed gushing from the very heart of womanhood. A crimson flush was glowing on her cheek, that had been long so pale. Her sex, her youth, and the whole richness of her beauty, came back from what men call the irrevocable past, and clustered themselves, with her maiden hope, and a happiness before unknown, within the magic circle of this hour. And, as if the gloom of the earth and sky had been but the effluence of these two mortal hearts, it vanished with their sorrow. All at once, as with a sudden smile of heaven, forth burst the sunshine, pouring a very flood into the obscure forest, gladdening each green leaf, transmuting the yellow fallen ones to gold, and gleaming adown the gray trunks of the solemn trees. The objects that had made a shadow hitherto, embodied the brightness now. The course of the little brook might be traced by its merry gleam afar into the wood’s heart of mystery, which had become a mystery of joy.
base: With the stigma gone, Hester felt a deep release. The weight of shame and pain lifted from her. She hadn’t realized how much she’d been carrying until she was free. She took off the cap that had kept her hair bound. Her hair fell over her shoulders, dark and thick. The contrast of shadow and light softened her face. A gentle smile came to her lips and stayed in her eyes. It showed she was connected to her femininity. A warm color returned to her cheeks, which had been pale for a long time. Parts of her identity—her youth, her beauty—came back from what people thought was lost. They mixed with her hope and a new kind of happiness. The heavy feeling of the earth and sky faded along with their sorrow. Then, as if touched by a divine light, the sun broke through. It filled the dark forest with brightness. Every green leaf shimmered. The yellow leaves turned gold. The gray trees glowed. Things that had cast shadows now had light. The little brook’s path could be seen by the way it sparkled as it moved through the woods, now a place of joy.
