The question is whether the government should do, or aid men to do, certain things, instead of leaving them to do them, either alone, or by their own voluntary co-operation. It is a question concerning the proper degree of government interference in men's lives. It is a question concerning the balance between individual liberty and the advantages of government interference.

title: On Liberty
input:
There exists a realm of action where society, as a collective, tends to have only an indirect interest, which includes aspects of a person's life and behavior that primarily impact themselves. While it is possible that these aspects may also affect others, this occurs only with their free and informed consent and participation. When referring to affecting oneself, it is important to note that this is in a direct and initial sense; what influences an individual may subsequently influence others through that individual. This potential for broader impact will be addressed later. Thus, this area represents the appropriate domain of personal liberty. 

It encompasses, first, the inner realm of consciousness, which calls for freedom of conscience in a broad sense. This includes the freedom to think and feel, as well as complete freedom of opinion and sentiment on all matters, whether practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The freedom to express and share opinions might appear to be governed by a different principle, since it pertains to an individual’s actions that involve others. However, it is often almost as significant as the freedom of thought itself and is largely based on similar reasoning, making it practically inseparable from it. Second, this principle advocates for the liberty of personal tastes and pursuits, allowing individuals to design their lives according to their own characters and to act as they wish, provided that their actions do not harm others, regardless of whether those others may perceive their choices as unwise or misguided. Third, from this individual liberty arises the freedom to form associations among individuals, enabling them to unite for any purpose that does not cause harm to others, assuming that those involved are of legal age and are not coerced or misled. In summary, the domain of human liberty encompasses individual thought, expression, personal pursuits, and the freedom to associate, all under the condition that these do not harm others.
human: But there is a sphere of action in which society, as distinguished from the individual, has, if any, only an indirect interest; comprehending all that portion of a person's life and conduct which affects only himself, or if it also affects others, only with their free, voluntary, and undeceived consent and participation. When I say only himself, I mean directly, and in the first instance: for whatever affects himself, may affect others through himself; and the objection which may be grounded on this contingency, will receive consideration in the sequel. This, then, is the appropriate region of human liberty. It comprises, first, the inward domain of consciousness; demanding liberty of conscience, in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological. The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions may seem to fall under a different principle, since it belongs to that part of the conduct of an individual which concerns other people; but, being almost of as much importance as the liberty of thought itself, and resting in great part on the same reasons, is practically inseparable from it. Secondly, the principle requires liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow: without impediment from our fellow-creatures, so long as what we do does not harm them, even though they should think our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong. Thirdly, from this liberty of each individual, follows the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite, for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived.
base:
There is a space where society as a whole isn’t directly involved, and it includes parts of a person’s life that mainly affect themselves. These parts might also affect others, but only if those others agree and are aware. When it comes to things that affect a person directly, it’s the start of a chain. What influences one person can later influence others through that person. That bigger effect will come up later. So this is where personal freedom belongs.

It starts with the inner world of a person’s mind, which needs freedom of thought and feeling. That includes the right to think and feel whatever they want, and to have any opinions on any subject—practical, scientific, moral, or religious. The right to talk about those opinions might seem different because it involves others. But it’s just as important as the right to think, and it’s based on the same reasons. So it’s almost like one without the other. Next, there’s the right to choose what you like and do what you want, as long as it doesn’t hurt others. Others might not see your choices as good, but that doesn’t matter. Finally, people can join together for any purpose as long as it doesn’t hurt others, and as long as they’re old enough and not forced or tricked. In short, freedom includes thinking, speaking, choosing what to do, and joining with others, as long as it doesn’t hurt anyone.
finetuned:
There is a world of action where society, as a whole, has only an indirect interest, - interests in a man's life and conduct which touch him alone, and may touch others only with their free consent and participation. When we speak of affecting himself, we mean it in the immediate and original sense; what affects him may affect others by him. This wider influence will be considered hereafter. So this is the sphere of individual liberty.

It is, first, the inner world of consciousness, requiring liberty of conscience in the widest sense - liberty to think and to feel, liberty of opinion and sentiment in all matters, practical, speculative, scientific, moral, or theological, complete. Liberty of expression and communication, which might seem to be governed by a different principle, since it relates to an individual's action towards others, is almost as important as the liberty of thought itself, and is mainly based on the same reasoning, and is practically inseparable from it. Second, it is the liberty of personal taste and pursuit, requiring that a man should design his life after his own character, and act as he likes, provided that his action injures no one, however much others may consider his choice as unwise or mistaken. Third, from this individual liberty comes the liberty to form associations among men, to combine together for any purpose which does not injure others, supposing that those concerned are of age, and are not compelled or misled.

title: On Liberty
input: It is worth noting that there exist numerous acts which, while they may only cause direct harm to the individuals who engage in them, should not be subject to legal prohibition. However, when such acts are performed in public, they constitute a breach of social decorum and, consequently, may be legitimately restricted under the category of offenses against others. Offenses against decency exemplify this concept; further elaboration on these matters is unnecessary, particularly since they are only tangentially related to our primary topic. The objection to public display is equally applicable to many actions that are not inherently reprehensible or perceived as such.
human: Again, there are many acts which, being directly injurious only to the agents themselves, ought not to be legally interdicted, but which, if done publicly, are a violation of good manners and coming thus within the category of offences against others may rightfully be prohibited. Of this kind are offences against decency; on which it is unnecessary to dwell, the rather as they are only connected indirectly with our subject, the objection to publicity being equally strong in the case of many actions not in themselves condemnable, nor supposed to be so.
base: Many actions cause harm only to those who do them and shouldn’t be illegal. But when done in public, they break social rules and can be properly restricted as offenses against others. Examples like offenses against decency show this. There’s no need to go into more detail, since they’re only loosely connected to our main point. The same argument applies to many actions that aren’t really bad or seen that way.
finetuned: There are many acts which, though they do no harm to any but those who commit them, ought not to be made criminal. But when such acts are done in public, they are an insult to the feelings of the community, and may, therefore, be properly included among offenses against others. Offenses against decency are the best example of this kind; there is no occasion for further discussion, especially as they have no real bearing on our subject. The same objection applies to many actions which are not themselves vicious, or are not so regarded.

title: The Time Machine
input:
You must follow my reasoning with considerable care. It is worth noting that I shall have to challenge one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted. For instance, the geometry that they taught you at school is founded upon a misconception.

Furthermore, is it not rather a substantial matter to expect us to begin upon? said Filby, an argumentative person with red hair.

Moreover, I do not mean to ask you to accept anything without reasonable ground for it. Additionally, you will soon concede as much as I require from you. It is worth noting that you know of course that a mathematical line, a line of no thickness, has no real existence. They taught you that? In essence, neither has a mathematical plane. These things are mere abstractions.

title: The Time Machine
input: Doubts began to arise, causing trouble. The question of why the Morlocks had taken the Time Machine came to mind, as it seemed likely they were responsible. This highlights the uncertainty surrounding the situation. Additionally, if the Eloi were indeed in a position of power, it was unclear why they could not return the machine. Furthermore, their intense fear of the dark was puzzling. In an attempt to gather more information, questions were posed to Weena about the Underworld. However, this line of inquiry was unsuccessful, as she initially failed to comprehend the questions and later refused to respond. The topic appeared to be unbearable for her, causing her to shiver. When pressed for answers, she became overwhelmed and cried. This suggests that the subject was deeply distressing for her. These tears were a rare sight in this era, and the only ones seen, apart from those of the narrator. Upon witnessing her distress, concern for the Morlocks subsided, and the focus shifted to comforting Weena. Ultimately, her tears were soon replaced with smiles and laughter, as a simple act, such as burning a match, was able to lift her spirits.
human: “Then came troublesome doubts. Why had the Morlocks taken my Time Machine? For I felt sure it was they who had taken it. Why, too, if the Eloi were masters, could they not restore the machine to me? And why were they so terribly afraid of the dark? I proceeded, as I have said, to question Weena about this Underworld, but here again I was disappointed. At first she would not understand my questions, and presently she refused to answer them. She shivered as though the topic was unendurable. And when I pressed her, perhaps a little harshly, she burst into tears. They were the only tears, except my own, I ever saw in that Golden Age. When I saw them I ceased abruptly to trouble about the Morlocks, and was only concerned in banishing these signs of her human inheritance from Weena’s eyes. And very soon she was smiling and clapping her hands, while I solemnly burnt a match.

If the Eloi were in charge, why couldn’t they give the machine back? Their fear of the dark didn’t make sense. To find out more, the narrator asked Weena about the Underworld. But she didn’t get it at first. Then she refused to answer. The topic was too much for her. She shivered. When pressed, she broke down and cried. That was rare back then. Only the narrator had seen tears before. Seeing her cry, worry about the Morlocks faded. The focus turned to helping Weena. Soon, her tears turned into smiles and laughter. A simple thing, like lighting a match, made her happy again.

And why the Eloi, if they were masters, could not send it back? And why they were so afraid of the dark? He asked Weena questions about the Underworld. She did not understand them at first, and then she would not answer them. The subject was unbearable for her, and she shivered. When he asked her why she shivered, she burst into tears. There were no tears in this age, except those of the narrator. He did not like to see her cry, and the thought of the Morlocks faded out. He comforted Weena. She was soon smiling and laughing again, for even to burn a match would brighten her face.

title: The War of the Worlds
input: I travel to London and observe the bustling crowds on Fleet Street and the Strand. It occurs to me that they are merely the phantoms of the past, haunting the thoroughfares that I have witnessed as silent and forlorn. These figures move back and forth, mere specters in a lifeless city, embodying a mockery of existence within a reanimated form. Furthermore, it is a peculiar experience to stand on Primrose Hill, as I did just one day prior to composing this final chapter. I behold the vast expanse of houses, appearing dim and blue through the haze of smoke and mist, gradually disappearing into the indistinct lower sky. I observe people strolling amidst the flower beds on the hill and sightseers gathered around the Martian machine that remains stationary. I hear the joyous noise of children at play and reflect on the time when I perceived all these sights as bright and distinct, sharp and silent, beneath the dawn of that last significant day.
human: I go to London and see the busy multitudes in Fleet Street and the Strand, and it comes across my mind that they are but the ghosts of the past, haunting the streets that I have seen silent and wretched, going to and fro, phantasms in a dead city, the mockery of life in a galvanised body. And strange, too, it is to stand on Primrose Hill, as I did but a day before writing this last chapter, to see the great province of houses, dim and blue through the haze of the smoke and mist, vanishing at last into the vague lower sky, to see the people walking to and fro among the flower beds on the hill, to see the sight-seers about the Martian machine that stands there still, to hear the tumult of playing children, and to recall the time when I saw it all bright and clear-cut, hard and silent, under the dawn of that last great day....

I see the big houses, dim and blue through the smoke and mist, fading into the blurry sky. I watch people walk in the flower beds and tourists around the Martian machine that doesn't move. I hear the laughter of children playing and think about when I saw all this as bright and clear, under the dawn of that last important day.

title: The War of the Worlds
input: At around six in the evening, I sat with my wife in the summerhouse, discussing the imminent battle with fervor. Suddenly, I heard a muffled explosion coming from the common, followed swiftly by a barrage of gunfire. Soon after, a violent crash reverberated nearby, shaking the ground beneath us. As I stepped onto the lawn, I witnessed the treetops near the Oriental College erupt in a smoky red flame, while the tower of the adjacent church collapsed into ruins. The pinnacle of the mosque had completely disappeared, and the roofline of the college appeared as though it had been struck by a heavy artillery shell. One of our chimneys cracked with a sound resembling a gunshot, then broke apart, sending debris tumbling onto the tiles and creating a pile of shattered red fragments on the flower bed beside my study window.
human: About six in the evening, as I sat at tea with my wife in the summerhouse talking vigorously about the battle that was lowering upon us, I heard a muffled detonation from the common, and immediately after a gust of firing. Close on the heels of that came a violent rattling crash, quite close to us, that shook the ground; and, starting out upon the lawn, I saw the tops of the trees about the Oriental College burst into smoky red flame, and the tower of the little church beside it slide down into ruin. The pinnacle of the mosque had vanished, and the roof line of the college itself looked as if a hundred-ton gun had been at work upon it. One of our chimneys cracked as if a shot had hit it, flew, and a piece of it came clattering down the tiles and made a heap of broken red fragments upon the flower bed by my study window.

Soon after, a loud crash shook the ground. I stepped onto the lawn and saw the trees near the Oriental College burning red with smoke. The church tower collapsed. The mosque's top was gone. The college's roof looked like it had been hit by a shell. One of our chimneys cracked like a gun shot, then broke, sending pieces onto the tiles and making a pile of red shards by my study window.

I went out upon the lawn, and saw the treetops close to the Oriental College blaze in a smoke-red flame, while the tower of the adjoining church was in ruins, and the pinnacle of the mosque had disappeared. The roof-line of the college looked as if it had been shot through by a shell. One of our chimneys cracked like a shot, then broke down, and all the fragments fell on the tiles, and piled up a heap of broken red shrapnel on the flower-beds beside my study-window.

title: The War of the Worlds
input:
The artilleryman shared his observations about the types of individuals who still remained in London. 

"Not long ago," he mentioned, "some individuals managed to restore the electric lights, resulting in Regent Street and the Circus being brightly lit and filled with intoxicated individuals, both men and women, who appeared to be celebrating and making noise until dawn. This was recounted to me by someone who witnessed it. As daylight approached, they noticed a fighting-machine nearby the Langham, observing them. It’s unclear how long it had been there, but it likely startled some of the people present. The machine then moved down the street and collected nearly a hundred individuals who were either too inebriated or frightened to escape." 

In summary, the artilleryman painted a picture of a chaotic scene marked by both celebration and fear in the city.
human:
The artilleryman began to tell me of the sort of people who still remained in London.

“One night last week,” he said, “some fools got the electric light in order, and there was all Regent Street and the Circus ablaze, crowded with painted and ragged drunkards, men and women, dancing and shouting till dawn. A man who was there told me. And as the day came they became aware of a fighting-machine standing near by the Langham and looking down at them. Heaven knows how long he had been there. It must have given some of them a nasty turn. He came down the road towards them, and picked up nearly a hundred too drunk or frightened to run away.”

As day came, they saw a fighting-machine near the Langham watching them. It’s not clear how long it had been there, but it probably scared some people. The machine then moved down the street and picked up nearly a hundred people who were too drunk or too scared to run." 

In short, the artilleryman described a city full of chaos, with both celebration and fear.

title: The War of the Worlds
input:
The ship was moving at a rapid pace, and within a short time, it appeared to be roughly halfway between the steamboat and the Martians. It was a dark shape against the vast, horizontal expanse of the Essex coast, which was gradually receding into the distance. 

Meanwhile, the lead Martian suddenly lowered its tube and released a canister of black gas at the ironclad vessel. The canister struck the ship's left side and deflected off in a dark, fluid motion that flowed away in a seaward direction. Consequently, a large amount of black smoke emerged, and the ironclad was able to move clear of it. At this point, the observers on the steamer, who were positioned low in the water and had the sun in their eyes, perceived the ironclad as being already close to the Martians.

She was steaming at such a pace that in a minute she seemed halfway between the steamboat and the Martians - a diminishing black bulk against the receding horizontal expanse of the Essex coast.

Suddenly the foremost Martian lowered his tube and discharged a canister of the black gas at the ironclad. It hit her larboard side and glanced off in an inky jet that rolled away to seaward, an unfolding torrent of Black Smoke, from which the ironclad drove clear. To the watchers from the steamer, low in the water and with the sun in their eyes, it seemed as though she were already among the Martians.

A lot of black smoke came up, and the ironclad managed to get clear of it. Then the people on the steamer, who were low in the water and had the sun in their eyes, saw the ironclad as being right near the Martians.

title: The War of the Worlds
input: Unable to discern the situation from his window, my brother decided to step outside into the street just as the sky began to brighten with dawn's early light. The number of people rushing by, both on foot and in vehicles, seemed to increase with each passing moment. He heard shouts of “Black Smoke!” echoing through the crowd, and the repetition of such a widespread fear was likely to be contagious. As my brother stood uncertainly on the doorstep, he noticed another newsvendor approaching and quickly purchased a paper. The vendor was hurrying away with the others, selling his papers for a shilling each as he ran, reflecting a strange mixture of urgency and commerce. In summary, the scene captured the chaotic atmosphere of the moment, blending fear and the instinct to profit.
human: Unable from his window to learn what was happening, my brother went down and out into the street, just as the sky between the parapets of the houses grew pink with the early dawn. The flying people on foot and in vehicles grew more numerous every moment. “Black Smoke!” he heard people crying, and again “Black Smoke!” The contagion of such a unanimous fear was inevitable. As my brother hesitated on the door-step, he saw another newsvendor approaching, and got a paper forthwith. The man was running away with the rest, and selling his papers for a shilling each as he ran - a grotesque mingling of profit and panic.

More people were moving around the street, walking and in cars, getting busier every minute. He heard someone yell “Black Smoke!” and the way people kept saying it made him feel uneasy. Standing on the doorstep, he saw another newsboy coming and bought a paper. The vendor was running off, selling each paper for a shilling, moving fast like everyone else. It was a mix of fear and trying to make money.

Standing irresolutely on the doorstep, he saw another newsvendor coming up and bought a paper. The man was running away with the rest, selling his papers at a shilling each as he ran, a curious blend of business and hurry.

title: The War of the Worlds
input:
By 8:00, a group of boys and unemployed men had already headed to the common to catch a glimpse of the "dead men from Mars," which is how the story was being told. This highlights the rapid spread of the news. I first heard about it from my newspaper boy at around 8:45 when I went to pick up my Daily Chronicle. I was understandably startled and quickly made my way to the sand-pits, crossing the Ottershaw bridge to get there. 

Upon arrival, I found a small crowd of around 20 people gathered around the large hole where the cylinder was located. The cylinder's appearance was imposing, as I have previously described, and it was embedded in the ground. The surrounding turf and gravel appeared to be charred, suggesting that the cylinder's impact had caused a brief, intense fire. This suggests that the heat generated by the impact was significant. Henderson and Ogilvy were not present at the scene. Ultimately, they likely realized that there was nothing to be done at that moment and had gone to Henderson's house for breakfast.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
input: Atalanta is not the first or the last maiden whom greed for gold has led to defile the temple of Love. Moreover, it is not only maidens but also men who, in the race of life, sink from the high and generous ideals of youth to the gambler's code of the stock exchange. In all our nation's striving, is the Gospel of Work not corrupted by the Gospel of Pay? This is so common that one half of people consider it normal. It is so unquestioned that we almost fear to ask whether the end of racing is gold and whether the proper aim of man is to be rich. If this is the fault of America, how dire a danger lies before a new land and a new city, lest Atlanta, stooping for mere gold, shall find that gold accursed.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
input: I have so far attempted to clarify the physical, economic, and political relations between Negroes and whites in the South as I have understood them, including crime and education for the reasons already given. Yet beyond these more tangible matters of human contact, there remains an essential part of any proper description of the South that is difficult to describe or define in terms easily understood by outsiders. It is, in short, the atmosphere of the land, the thought and feeling, and the countless small actions that together constitute daily life. In any community or nation, these small things are the most elusive to grasp and yet the most essential to a clear understanding of group life as a whole. What is true of all communities is especially true of the South, where, beyond written history and printed law, there has been unfolding for a generation a profound storm and stress of human souls, an intense ferment of feeling, and an intricate writhing of spirit such as few peoples have experienced. Within and beyond the somber veil of color, vast social forces have been at work: efforts for human betterment, movements toward disintegration and despair, tragedies and comedies in social and economic life, and a shifting and rising and falling of human hearts that have made this land one of mingled sorrow and joy, of change and excitement and unrest.
human: I have thus far sought to make clear the physical, economic, and political relations of the Negroes and whites in the South, as I have conceived them, including, for the reasons set forth, crime and education. But after all that has been said on these more tangible matters of human contact, there still remains a part essential to a proper description of the South which it is difficult to describe or fix in terms easily understood by strangers. It is, in fine, the atmosphere of the land, the thought and feeling, the thousand and one little actions which go to make up life. In any community or nation it is these little things which are most elusive to the grasp and yet most essential to any clear conception of the group life taken as a whole. Within and without the sombre veil of color vast social forces have been at work, - efforts for human betterment, movements toward disintegration and despair, tragedies and comedies in social and economic life, and a swaying and lifting and sinking of human hearts which have made this land a land of mingled sorrow and joy, of change and excitement and unrest.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
input: The discovery of the golden fleece signifies a notable development; it has not only been located but is also being produced in its region of origin. The operation of cotton mills represents a significant aspect of the modern economy in the New South. Throughout the Carolinas and Georgia, extending into Mexico, one can observe the presence of these large, utilitarian structures, which, despite their simple appearance, are characterized by a bustling and noisy activity that contrasts with the surrounding landscape. This suggests that the Cotton Kingdom continues to play an important role, as its influence persists. Furthermore, markets that once resisted newcomers have gradually expanded overseas and have begun to move toward the Black Belt region, indicating a shift in economic dynamics.
human: And now the golden fleece is found; not only found, but, in its birthplace, woven. For the hum of the cotton-mills is the newest and most significant thing in the New South to-day. All through the Carolinas and Georgia, away down to Mexico, rise these gaunt red buildings, bare and homely, and yet so busy and noisy withal that they scarce seem to belong to the slow and sleepy land. Perhaps they sprang from dragons’ teeth. So the Cotton Kingdom still lives; the world still bows beneath her sceptre. Even the markets that once defied the parvenu have crept one by one across the seas, and then slowly and reluctantly, but surely, have started toward the Black Belt.

title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
input: The besiegers, perhaps unsettled by the chaos they had just caused and the sudden silence that followed, instinctively stepped back and looked inside. Before them, in the gentle light of the lamp, was a cabinet, with a warm fire flickering and crackling in the hearth, the kettle softly whistling a delicate tune. A few drawers were ajar, and papers were neatly arranged on the business table, while closer to the fire, items were prepared for tea. It was likely the quietest room one might imagine, and, aside from the glass-fronted cabinets filled with chemicals, it could be described as one of the most ordinary spaces that night in London. Overall, it presented a striking contrast to the turmoil outside.

title: The strange case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
input: Men have historically engaged others to carry out their illicit activities while maintaining their own safety and reputation. This highlights a unique phenomenon in which I was the first to employ this practice for personal enjoyment. I was able to navigate public life with an air of respectability, and, in an instant, shed that façade to embrace a sense of freedom. Ultimately, I found complete security in my concealed existence. This suggests a profound detachment; I did not even have to take direct responsibility for my actions. By simply retreating to my laboratory, allowing myself a brief moment to prepare and consume a concoction that I always kept at hand, I could make Edward Hyde disappear as easily as a breath vanishes from a mirror. In his place, I would quietly return home, tending to my studies with a sense of assurance that allowed me to dismiss any doubts about my character.
human: Men have before hired bravos to transact their crimes, while their own person and reputation sat under shelter. I was the first that ever did so for his pleasures. I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability, and in a moment, like a schoolboy, strip off these lendings and spring headlong into the sea of liberty. But for me, in my impenetrable mantle, the safety was complete. Think of it - I did not even exist! Let me but escape into my laboratory door, give me but a second or two to mix and swallow the draught that I had always standing ready; and whatever he had done, Edward Hyde would pass away like the stain of breath upon a mirror; and there in his stead, quietly at home, trimming the midnight lamp in his study, a man who could afford to laugh at suspicion, would be Henry Jekyll.
base: Men have long hired others to do their wrongdoings while keeping themselves safe and respected. I was the first to use this method for my own pleasure. I moved through public life with dignity, then in a moment, I dropped that image and felt free. In the end, I found safety in hiding. This shows a deep separation; I didn’t even have to be responsible for what I did. All I had to do was go to my lab, take a moment to prepare and drink the potion I always kept ready. Then Edward Hyde would vanish as easily as breath from a mirror. In his place, I would go home quietly, taking care of my studies with the confidence that let me ignore any questions about who I was.

I did not even have to take the responsibility; for by retreating to my laboratory, and taking a little time to dress and drink the draught which I always kept ready, I could make Hyde disappear as easily as a breath goes out of a mirror. Then I should quietly go home and study again, with the assurance of a conscience that would let me throw off any suspicion of my character.

input: A careful observer might have noticed that the subject was unpleasant; however, the doctor addressed it cheerfully. "My poor Utterson," he remarked, "you are unfortunate to have such a client. Nevertheless, he is still a rigid scholar, an uninformed and loud scholar. I have never been more let down by any man than I have been by Lanyon."

input: I suppose I must finish my lessons first. I will not allow myself to open that new book Jane lent me until I am through. However, it is a terrible temptation, Matthew. You must not give it to me, Matthew, until my lessons are done, not even if I implore you on my bended knees. It is all very well to say resist temptation, but it is ever so much easier to resist it if you cannot get the key. And then shall I run down the cellar and get some russets, Matthew? input: Anne expressed her determination to engage with young girls respectfully, emphasizing that she would not laugh at their use of complex vocabulary, as she recognized the emotional impact this could have. During the process, Diana left Anne to stir while she prepared the plates, leading to the taffy burning. Additionally, a cat walked across one plate, resulting in its disposal. Despite these setbacks, Anne found the activity to be enjoyable. Upon returning home, Mrs. Barry invited Anne to visit frequently, while Diana affectionately waved goodbye from the window. I know from sorrowful experience how that hurts one’s feelings. After tea Diana and I made taffy. The taffy wasn’t very good, I suppose because neither Diana nor I had ever made any before. “I cannot think of anything worse,” Marilla reflected as she nervously shelled peas. “I do not believe she intended to steal it. She probably took it to play with or to fuel her imagination. It is obvious she must have taken it, as no one else had been in that room since she left, according to her own account, until I went up tonight. The brooch is undoubtedly missing. I assume she has lost it and is too frightened to admit it for fear of punishment. It is upsetting to consider that she tells lies. This is a far more serious issue than her earlier temper. It is a heavy burden to care for a child whom one cannot trust. Deception and dishonesty are what she has shown. I must admit I feel worse about that than about the brooch itself. If she had only told the truth, I would not feel as troubled.”

input:

One evening, Marilla returned from the orchard carrying a basket of apples and discovered Anne sitting by the east window in the fading light, crying uncontrollably.

"It is about Diana," Anne sobbed dramatically. "I love Diana so much, Marilla. I cannot imagine living without her. However, I know that as we grow older, Diana will marry and leave me. What will I do then? I detest her husband; I truly despise him. I have envisioned the entire event—the wedding and everything. Diana will be dressed in white, adorned with a veil, looking as beautiful and regal as a queen, while I will stand as the bridesmaid in a lovely dress with puffed sleeves, concealing a broken heart beneath my smiling exterior. Then I will have to say goodbye to Diana…" At this point, Anne completely broke down and wept with escalating sorrow.

title: The Age of Innocence
input:
She regarded him with a hint of her former sharpness. "Do you think this might be risky?" 

"But unconventional? I understand; it likely is," he replied. She paused for a moment, reflecting. "I hadn’t considered it, as I have just engaged in something quite a bit more unusual." A slight touch of irony seemed to linger in her gaze. "I have just chosen not to reclaim a sum of money that rightfully belonged to me."

Archer stood up and took a few steps away from her. She had closed her parasol and was lightly tracing patterns in the gravel. After a short while, he returned and positioned himself in front of her.

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
input:
Folklore, legends, myths, and fairy tales have accompanied childhood throughout history, as every vibrant child possesses a natural and profound appreciation for extraordinary, enchanting, and evidently unreal narratives. The winged fairies depicted by the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen have undoubtedly delivered more joy to youthful hearts than any other human creation.

Moreover, the traditional fairy tale, having fulfilled its purpose for countless generations, may now be regarded as “historical” within the children’s literary canon. title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: It is worth noting that the reason it is natural to refer to this principle as a law of thought lies in the fact that we rely on thought, rather than external observation, to convince ourselves of its necessary truth. After we have observed that a tree is a beech, we do not need to examine it again to confirm that it is not also a beech; our reasoning alone informs us that such a contradiction is impossible. However, the conclusion that the law of contradiction is solely a law of thought is, in fact, erroneous. When we accept the law of contradiction, we do not assert that the mind is constructed in such a way that it must adhere to this law. Rather, this acceptance emerges as a subsequent outcome of psychological reflection, which itself presupposes an initial belief in the law of contradiction. The belief in this law pertains to the nature of reality and not merely to the realm of thought. It is not, for example, the conviction that if we consider a specific tree to be a beech, we cannot simultaneously consider it to be not a beech; instead, it is the assertion that if the tree is a beech, it cannot concurrently be not a beech. Consequently, the law of contradiction pertains to the nature of things rather than merely to thoughts; while the belief in the law of contradiction qualifies as a thought, the law itself constitutes a fact regarding the entities in the world. If the assertion we make when we accept the law of contradiction were not true concerning the nature of reality, the necessity of our belief would not render the law of contradiction true; this indicates that the law cannot be classified solely as a law of thought.
human: Now what makes it natural to call this principle a law of thought is that it is by thought rather than by outward observation that we persuade ourselves of its necessary truth. When we have seen that a tree is a beech, we do not need to look again in order to ascertain whether it is also not a beech; thought alone makes us know that this is impossible. But the conclusion that the law of contradiction is a law of thought is nevertheless erroneous. What we believe, when we believe the law of contradiction, is not that the mind is so made that it must believe the law of contradiction. This belief is a subsequent result of psychological reflection, which presupposes the belief in the law of contradiction. The belief in the law of contradiction is a belief about things, not only about thoughts. It is not, e.g., the belief that if we think a certain tree is a beech, we cannot at the same time think that it is not a beech; it is the belief that if the tree is a beech, it cannot at the same time be not a beech. Thus the law of contradiction is about things, and not merely about thoughts; and although belief in the law of contradiction is a thought, the law of contradiction itself is not a thought, but a fact concerning the things in the world. If this, which we believe when we believe the law of contradiction, were not true of the things in the world, the fact that we were compelled to think it true would not save the law of contradiction from being false; and this shows that the law is not a law of thought.

title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: In derivative knowledge, it is essential that our ultimate premises possess a certain degree of self-evidence, as must the connection between these premises and the conclusions derived from them. For instance, consider a reasoning process in geometry. It is insufficient for the axioms upon which we base our reasoning to be self-evident; it is equally necessary that, at each stage of the reasoning, the relationship between premises and conclusions be self-evident as well. In complex reasoning, this connection often exhibits only a minimal degree of self-evidence; consequently, errors in reasoning are not unlikely when the difficulty of the task is considerable.
human: In derivative knowledge our ultimate premisses must have some degree of self-evidence, and so must their connexion with the conclusions deduced from them. Take for example a piece of reasoning in geometry. It is not enough that the axioms from which we start should be self-evident: it is necessary also that, at each step in the reasoning, the connexion of premiss and conclusion should be self-evident. In difficult reasoning, this connexion has often only a very small degree of self-evidence; hence errors of reasoning are not improbable where the difficulty is great.

Just because the basic rules are obvious doesn’t mean the steps in between are. In complicated reasoning, those links are often only slightly clear. That means mistakes are more likely when the work gets tough.

title: The Problems of Philosophy
input: If the previous account holds some validity, it appears that our understanding of truths may largely depend on our intuitive knowledge. As such, it seems worthwhile to explore the nature and extent of intuitive knowledge, similar to how we previously examined knowledge by acquaintance. However, knowledge of truths introduces an additional challenge that does not typically arise with knowledge of objects: the issue of error. It can often happen that some of our beliefs are mistaken, which leads us to consider how we might distinguish knowledge from error, if it is possible at all. This concern is not present in the context of knowledge by acquaintance, since, regardless of the specific object of acquaintance, even in cases like dreams and hallucinations, no error occurs as long as we focus on the immediate object. Error tends to arise only when we interpret the immediate object, or sense-datum, as indicative of some external physical object. Therefore, the challenges associated with knowledge of truths may be more complex than those linked to knowledge of objects. To begin addressing the issues related to knowledge of truths, let us first investigate the nature and scope of our intuitive judgments.

Some of our beliefs turn out to be erroneous, and therefore it becomes necessary to consider how, if at all, we can distinguish knowledge from error. This problem does not arise with regard to knowledge by acquaintance, for, whatever may be the object of acquaintance, even in dreams and hallucinations, there is no error involved so long as we do not go beyond the immediate object: error can only arise when we regard the immediate object, i.e. the sense-datum, as the mark of some physical object. Thus the problems connected with knowledge of truths are more difficult than those connected with knowledge of things. As the first of the problems connected with knowledge of truths, let us examine the nature and scope of our intuitive judgements.

Error comes in when we take what we experience as signs of something real. So the difficulties with knowing truths might be tougher than those with knowing objects. After a brief and somewhat unclear exchange, it became apparent that the reporter had heard Gatsby's name mentioned in his office, though he either chose not to disclose the context or did not fully grasp it. This was his day off, and he had taken the initiative to investigate further. 

While his approach was somewhat random, it suggested that the reporter's instincts were accurate. Gatsby's growing notoriety, fueled by the many guests who had enjoyed his hospitality and shared their experiences, had reached a level where he was nearly considered newsworthy. Various contemporary legends, such as the rumored "underground pipeline to Canada," became associated with him, and one persistent tale claimed he did not actually reside in a house, but rather in a boat designed to resemble a house, which was allegedly moved secretly along the Long Island coast. Ultimately, it remains unclear why these fabrications appealed to James Gatz from North Dakota.

title: The Great Gatsby
input: The appeal of New York lies in its vibrant nighttime atmosphere, characterized by a dynamic interplay of people and vehicles that captivates the observer. Walking along Fifth Avenue, one might find themselves drawn to the romantic figures in the crowd, imagining brief connections that go unnoticed by others. This act of imagination can extend to envisioning these individuals in their private lives, suggesting a fleeting intimacy that is both thrilling and elusive. However, amidst this enchanting urban twilight, there is also a sense of poignant loneliness that can be felt not only by oneself but also by others. The image of young clerks lingering in front of shop windows, waiting for their solitary meals, reflects the bittersweet nature of those moments, highlighting the contrast between the vibrancy of the city and the isolation experienced by some of its inhabitants.
human: I began to like New York, the racy, adventurous feel of it at night, and the satisfaction that the constant flicker of men and women and machines gives to the restless eye. I liked to walk up Fifth Avenue and pick out romantic women from the crowd and imagine that in a few minutes I was going to enter into their lives, and no one would ever know or disapprove. Sometimes, in my mind, I followed them to their apartments on the corners of hidden streets, and they turned and smiled back at me before they faded through a door into warm darkness. At the enchanted metropolitan twilight I felt a haunting loneliness sometimes, and felt it in others - poor young clerks who loitered in front of windows waiting until it was time for a solitary restaurant dinner - young clerks in the dusk, wasting the most poignant moments of night and life.
base: New York’s appeal is in its night life, where people and cars move together, making the city feel alive. On Fifth Avenue, you might notice couples in the crowd, and you wonder about their stories, the moments they share that others don’t see. You might imagine their lives, the quiet things they do alone. But in the middle of all that energy, there’s also a quiet sadness. You see young workers standing by store windows, waiting for their own meals, and it makes you think about how even in a busy city, some people feel alone. It’s a mix of excitement and loneliness, a feeling that’s everywhere but never quite spoken.

But there is also the lonely loneliness of it. There is the image of the young clerks waiting before shop windows for their solitary meals.

title: The Great Gatsby
input: The following April, Daisy welcomed the birth of her daughter, after which they relocated to France for a year. I encountered them one spring in Cannes, subsequently in Deauville, before they returned to Chicago to establish their permanent residence. As you are aware, Daisy enjoyed considerable popularity in Chicago. They mingled with a vibrant social circle, composed largely of affluent and youthful individuals who exhibited a penchant for exuberance; however, Daisy emerged with an impeccably pristine reputation. This may be attributed, at least in part, to her choice to abstain from alcohol. It is a significant advantage to refrain from drinking within a milieu characterized by heavy consumption, as it enables one to exercise discretion and, moreover, to time any personal indiscretions in such a way that they remain unnoticed or unaddressed by others. It is conceivable that Daisy never engaged in romantic affairs at all; nevertheless, there exists an undeniable allure in the quality of her voice.

title: The Great Gatsby
input: There was dancing taking place on the canvas in the garden, where older men might often be seen guiding young girls in circles that lacked grace, while couples, perhaps seeking to appear fashionable, held each other in somewhat awkward positions along the edges. Many single girls danced alone or took turns with the orchestra, giving the banjo or drums a brief rest. By midnight, the atmosphere had likely become even more festive. A well-known tenor sang in Italian, while a somewhat infamous contralto performed in a jazz style. In between musical numbers, people could be observed performing acts around the garden, accompanied by bursts of cheerful laughter rising into the warm summer night. A pair of performers, who turned out to be the girls in yellow, presented a playful act in costume. Champagne was served in glasses that were larger than typical finger bowls. As the moon rose higher, a shimmering triangle of silver scales appeared in the Sound, gently responding to the rhythmic sound of banjos played on the lawn. Overall, the scene was one of lively celebration and enjoyment.

title: The Great Gatsby
input:
At eight o'clock, the dark lanes of the Forties were filled with taxicabs, all of them heading towards the theatre district. These vehicles were lined up five deep, and the scene was one of intense activity. As the people in the taxis waited, they would often lean together, singing and laughing, while cigarettes glowed inside, creating circular patterns. Meanwhile, I couldn't help but feel a sense of melancholy. As I watched the taxicabs, I imagined that the people in them were rushing towards a night of enjoyment, and I found myself wishing them well.

Some time later, I lost track of Jordan Baker, but then I encountered her again in the middle of summer. Initially, I was pleased to be in her company, largely because she was a renowned golf champion. Her name was well known, and I felt flattered to be seen with her. However, my feelings towards her soon evolved into something more complex. Although I was not in love with her, I developed a certain tenderness and curiosity about her. The aloof expression she presented to the world seemed to conceal something, and I eventually discovered what it was. During a house party in Warwick, she borrowed a car and left it outside in the rain with the top down, and then she lied about it. This incident reminded me of a story about her that I had heard previously, but could not recall at the time. The story was related to a golf tournament, where she had been involved in a controversy surrounding the movement of her ball from a difficult position. The incident had almost become a scandal, but it eventually died down after a caddy retracted his statement and another witness admitted that he might have been mistaken. The details of the incident had remained in my mind, and they were now linked to her name.

title: The Great Gatsby
input:
One of the performers, dressed in shimmering opal, suddenly grabs a cocktail from midair, drinks it for courage, and begins to dance alone on the stage. This moment prompts a brief silence, after which the orchestra leader adjusts the rhythm to accommodate her performance. As word spreads that she is Gilda Gray’s understudy from the Follies, conversations begin to buzz, signaling that the festivities have commenced.

On my first visit to Gatsby's house, I realized I was among the few guests who had received a formal invitation. Most people were not invited in the traditional sense; instead, they traveled in cars to Long Island and found their way to Gatsby’s residence. Once there, they were introduced by acquaintances who knew Gatsby, and they acted according to the social norms typical of a lively amusement park. Many guests arrived and departed without ever meeting Gatsby, attending the party with an innocent enthusiasm that served as their entry pass.

title: Oliver Twist
input: Rose expressed her emotions to the doctor, indicating that her aunt had given him full authority over the situation. She requested that he not be excessively harsh on the individuals involved. The doctor responded by suggesting that Rose seemed to believe that everyone, apart from herself, was inclined to be unkind on that day. He commented that he hoped for the sake of young men that she would be found in a similarly sympathetic state when approached by a young man seeking her compassion. He added that he wished he were younger so he could take advantage of the present opportunity to do so.
human:
“Then my aunt invests you with full power,” said Rose, smiling through her tears; “but pray don’t be harder upon the poor fellows than is indispensably necessary.”

“You seem to think,” retorted the doctor, “that everybody is disposed to be hard-hearted today, except yourself, Miss Rose. I only hope, for the sake of the rising male sex generally, that you may be found in as vulnerable and soft-hearted a mood by the first eligible young fellow who appeals to your compassion; and I wish I were a young fellow, that I might avail myself, on the spot, of such a favourable opportunity for doing so, as the present.”

The doctor said it seemed like Rose thought everyone else was mean that day. He said he hoped, for the sake of young men, that she would be kind when a young man asked for her help. He added he wished he were younger so he could take advantage of the chance.

title: Oliver Twist
input: A slight commotion in the courtroom drew his attention back to the proceedings. He observed that the jurors had gathered to deliberate their verdict. As he scanned the gallery, he noted people straining to see his face; some were quickly adjusting their glasses, while others whispered to their neighbors, their expressions reflecting strong disapproval. A small number seemed indifferent to him and focused solely on the jury, appearing impatient with the delay. Ultimately, he found no expression of sympathy directed toward him in any of the faces present, including those of the many women in attendance. Instead, the prevailing sentiment was a keen interest in the possibility of his condemnation.
human: A slight bustle in the court, recalled him to himself. Looking round, he saw that the jurymen had turned together, to consider their verdict. As his eyes wandered to the gallery, he could see the people rising above each other to see his face: some hastily applying their glasses to their eyes: and others whispering their neighbours with looks expressive of abhorrence. A few there were, who seemed unmindful of him, and looked only to the jury, in impatient wonder how they could delay. But in no one face - not even among the women, of whom there were many there - could he read the faintest sympathy with himself, or any feeling but one of all-absorbing interest that he should be condemned.

Some were adjusting their glasses, others were talking to their friends, looking upset. A few didn’t seem to care and were just waiting for the jury. He didn’t see any faces showing he was sorry. The people there were more interested in whether he would be punished.

title: Oliver Twist
input:
He roamed across vast stretches of land yet always returned to the familiar place. Morning transitioned into noon, and the day began to fade. Despite this, he continued to wander back and forth, up and down, and around the same area. Eventually, he managed to leave and set his direction toward Hatfield. 

At nine o’clock in the evening, the man, exhausted, and the dog, limping from unusual exertion, descended the hill past the church of the peaceful village. They made their way along the narrow street and entered a small public house, its dim light guiding them to safety. A fire crackled in the tap-room, where several local laborers were gathered, enjoying their drinks.

Morning and noon had passed, and the day was on the wane, and still he rambled to and fro, and up and down, and round and round, and still lingered about the same spot. At last he got away, and shaped his course for Hatfield.

It was nine o’clock at night, when the man, quite tired out, and the dog, limping and lame from the unaccustomed exercise, turned down the hill by the church of the quiet village, and plodding along the little street, crept into a small public-house, whose scanty light had guided them to the spot. There was a fire in the tap-room, and some country-labourers were drinking before it.

title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Complete
input:
The bluff appears uniform from the cave hollow, with no houses or wood-yards and bushes that look the same. However, do you notice that white area up there where a landslide occurred? That is one of my markers. We will get ashore now.

Huck examined the surrounding area but found nothing. Tom confidently entered a dense cluster of sumach bushes and stated, "Money. You make them raise as much as they can from their friends, and after keeping them for a year, if they have not raised anything, you kill them. That is the general method. However, you do not kill the women. You simply confine them, but you do not harm them. They are always beautiful, wealthy, and extremely frightened. You take their watches and belongings, but you always remove your hat and speak courteously. There are no individuals as polite as robbers, as you will find in any book. Eventually, the women start to develop feelings for you. After spending one or two weeks in the cave, they cease crying, and you could not persuade them to leave. If you attempted to drive them out, they would immediately return. This is a common theme in all the books."

Huck searched all the place about, and found nothing. Tom proudly marched into a thick clump of sumach bushes and said:

“Money. You make them raise all they can, off’n their friends; and after you’ve kept them a year, if it ain’t raised then you kill them. That’s the general way. Only you don’t kill the women. You shut up the women, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and awfully scared. You take their watches and things, but you always take your hat off and talk polite. They ain’t anybody as polite as robbers - you’ll see that in any book. Well, the women get to loving you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two weeks they stop crying and after that you couldn’t get them to leave. If you drove them out they’d turn right around and come back. It’s so in all the books.”

Presently the women begin to fall in love with you. After spending one or two weeks in the cave they stop crying, and you couldn’t persuade them to go. If you tried to drive them out they’d come back right away. That’s the way in all the books.”

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
input: One night we captured a small section of a lumber raft, consisting of fine pine planks. It was twelve feet wide and approximately fifteen or sixteen feet long, and its surface stood six or seven inches above the water, forming a solid, level floor. Additionally, we could observe saw-logs drifting by during the daylight hours on occasion, but we allowed them to pass, as we did not reveal ourselves in daylight. Furthermore, on another night, while we were positioned near the head of the island just before daybreak, a frame house came floating down on the western side. It was a two-story structure and was tilted considerably. Moreover, we paddled out and boarded it, entering through an upstairs window. However, it was still too dark to see, so we secured the canoe and settled in it to await the arrival of daylight.

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
input: As I made my way up the bank, I kept a watchful eye out for my father and also paid attention to what the rising water might bring. Before long, a canoe came into view, and it was a particularly nice one, approximately thirteen or fourteen feet in length, floating effortlessly on the water. I quickly jumped into the water, fully clothed, and swam out to the canoe, as I may have expected to find someone hiding in it, trying to trick people, but that was not the case this time. The canoe was indeed empty and had been drifting, so I climbed aboard and paddled it to the shore. I thought to myself that my father would likely be pleased when he saw the canoe, as it could be worth around ten dollars. However, when I reached the shore, my father was nowhere to be seen, and as I was guiding the canoe into a small, secluded creek surrounded by vines and willows, I had another idea: I decided it would be a good idea to hide the canoe and, instead of heading into the woods when I ran away, I could travel down the river by about fifty miles and set up camp in one location, which can often make for a more comfortable experience than constantly walking on foot. In summary, my discovery of the canoe led me to consider a new plan for when I would eventually run away.

Well, all at once here comes a canoe; just a beauty, too, about thirteen or fourteen foot long, riding high like a duck. I shot head-first off of the bank like a frog, clothes and all on, and struck out for the canoe. I just expected there’d be somebody laying down in it, because people often done that to fool folks, and when a chap had pulled a skiff out most to it they’d raise up and laugh at him. But it warn’t so this time. It was a drift-canoe sure enough, and I clumb in and paddled her ashore. Thinks I, the old man will be glad when he sees this - she’s worth ten dollars. But when I got to shore pap wasn’t in sight yet, and as I was running her into a little creek like a gully, all hung over with vines and willows, I struck another idea: I judged I’d hide her good, and then, ’stead of taking to the woods when I run off, I’d go down the river about fifty mile and camp in one place for good, and not have such a rough time tramping on foot.

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
input: A month or two ago, when Peter first fell ill, he expressed a sense of resignation about his recovery. He was quite old, and George's daughters were too young to provide him with much companionship, apart from Mary Jane, the red-haired girl. After George and his wife passed away, Peter felt increasingly lonely and showed little desire to continue living. He had a strong wish to see Harvey and William, as he was the type of person who could not bring himself to draft a will. He left behind a letter addressed to Harvey, in which he indicated the location of his hidden money and outlined how he wanted the rest of his property distributed, ensuring that George's daughters would be taken care of, since George had left them with nothing. That letter was the only document Peter was willing to write.

He most desperately wanted to see Harvey - and William, too, for that matter - because he was one of them kind that can’t bear to make a will. He left a letter behind for Harvey, and said he’d told in it where his money was hid, and how he wanted the rest of the property divided up so George’s g’yirls would be all right - for George didn’t leave nothing. And that letter was all they could get him to put a pen to.”

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
input:
Laws knows that I may have wanted to visit Tom badly enough to consider going, and I had every intention to do so; however, after a certain point, I really wouldn’t have gone, even for great rewards. 

Yet, both she and Tom occupied my thoughts, leading to a rather restless night. I found myself wandering down the path twice during the night, quietly approaching the front. Each time, I noticed her sitting by the candle in the window, gazing down the road with tears in her eyes. I wished I could do something to help her, but I felt powerless, aside from promising myself that I would never again do anything to upset her. When I awoke at dawn for the third time and slipped back down, she was still there. Her candle was nearly extinguished, and her head was resting on her hand as she slept. In summary, my concern for her and my determination to avoid causing her distress were strong throughout the night.

“Here and here,” replied Catherine, as she struck one hand against her forehead and the other against her breast. “In whichever place the soul resides, I am convinced in both my soul and my heart that I am in error.” 

She settled herself beside me once more; her expression became increasingly somber and serious, and her clasped hands began to tremble. 

“Oh, do not, Miss Catherine!” I exclaimed. “We are already dismal enough without summoning ghosts and visions to trouble us. Come, let us be joyful and true to yourself! Observe little Hareton; he is not dreaming of anything gloomy. How sweetly he smiles in his sleep!”

input: Yes, if we can keep him, I thought to myself, though I had serious doubts that there was much hope of it. I then wondered how such a weak child could possibly live at Wuthering Heights, with his father and Hareton as his companions and teachers. I had just taken the children upstairs after tea and had seen Linton fall asleep—he would not let me leave until he was asleep—when I came back down and was standing by the table in the hall, lighting a bedroom candle for Mr. Edgar. At that moment, a maid came out of the kitchen and told me that Mr. Heathcliff’s servant Joseph was at the door and wished to speak with the master.

Hareton made no answer, but stared at his plate. Mr. Heathcliff glanced at him, and returned to his breakfast, and his thoughts. The rest of the meal passed off without accident; the young people, however, had been endeavouring to keep out of each other’s way. Just as we were finishing, Joseph burst in at the door, his quivering lip and furious eyes denoting that he had found out the damage done to his precious shrubs. He had seen Cathy and her cousin near the spot before he went to look at it, for he began to talk in a confused way, his jaws moving as if they were chewing cud.

title: Frankenstein
input: The old woman responded, "Regarding the gentleman in question, it may be beneficial for you to consider the potential consequences of your actions, as it's possible that things could become difficult for you. Nevertheless, that's not my concern; my role is to care for you and help you recover, which I will do to the best of my ability while maintaining a clear conscience - it would be beneficial if everyone could do the same. I turned away from the woman, feeling a sense of distaste towards her seemingly insensitive remarks, especially given my fragile state at the time. However, I was also feeling rather weak and struggled to process everything that had happened. My life experiences seemed somewhat surreal, and I can often find myself wondering if they actually occurred, as they tend to lack a sense of realism when I think back on them. In summary, the old woman's words had a profound impact on me, and I was left feeling uncertain and disconnected from my past.

“For that matter,” replied the old woman, “if you mean about the gentleman you murdered, I believe that it were better for you if you were dead, for I fancy it will go hard with you! However, that’s none of my business; I am sent to nurse you and get you well; I do my duty with a safe conscience; it were well if everybody did the same.”

I turned with loathing from the woman who could utter so unfeeling a speech to a person just saved, on the very edge of death; but I felt languid and unable to reflect on all that had passed. The whole series of my life appeared to me as a dream; I sometimes doubted if indeed it were all true, for it never presented itself to my mind with the force of reality.

title: Frankenstein
input: As I looked up, I saw the demon standing at the window, illuminated by the light of the moon. This sight caused me to tremble and my heart to fail within me. The demon's face was distorted by a gruesome smile as he stared at me, seated and engaged in the task that he had assigned to me. Meanwhile, it became clear that he had been following me throughout my travels. He had been lurking in forests, concealing himself in caves, and seeking refuge in vast and isolated areas of wilderness. Furthermore, he had now appeared to monitor my progress and demand that I fulfill the promise that I had made to him.

Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress and claim the fulfilment of my promise.

He had been in the woods, hiding in caves, and taking shelter in lonely parts of the wild. Now he was here, keeping an eye on me and asking me to keep my promise.

title: Frankenstein
input: While I was engaged in repairing the boat and organizing the sails, a group of individuals gathered nearby. They appeared surprised by my presence, but instead of providing help, they whispered to one another and gestured in a manner that could have caused concern under different circumstances. However, I noted that they were speaking English and chose to communicate with them in that language. I asked, "Could you please tell me the name of this town and where I am?"
human: As I was occupied in fixing the boat and arranging the sails, several people crowded towards the spot. They seemed much surprised at my appearance, but instead of offering me any assistance, whispered together with gestures that at any other time might have produced in me a slight sensation of alarm. As it was, I merely remarked that they spoke English, and I therefore addressed them in that language. “My good friends,” said I, “will you be so kind as to tell me the name of this town and inform me where I am?”

title: A Tale of Two Cities
input: The lion settled onto his back on a sofa beside the drinking table, while the jackal occupied his own cluttered table on the opposite side, equipped with bottles and glasses. Both engaged in drinking, but their approaches differed significantly. The lion lounged with his hands resting in his waistband, gazing at the fire or occasionally perusing lighter materials. In contrast, the jackal focused intently on his work, his brow furrowed, so immersed that he often struggled to find his glass, sometimes searching for over a minute before successfully locating it. Occasionally, the complexity of his task compelled the jackal to rise and refresh his towels. Upon returning from these trips to the jug and basin, he donned unusual and damp headgear, which appeared even more absurd given his serious demeanor. This highlights the contrasting behaviors of the two characters, reflecting their differing personalities and approaches to their task.
human: The lion then composed himself on his back on a sofa on one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal sat at his own paper-bestrewn table proper, on the other side of it, with the bottles and glasses ready to his hand. Both resorted to the drinking-table without stint, but each in a different way; the lion for the most part reclining with his hands in his waistband, looking at the fire, or occasionally flirting with some lighter document; the jackal, with knitted brows and intent face, so deep in his task, that his eyes did not even follow the hand he stretched out for his glass - which often groped about, for a minute or more, before it found the glass for his lips. Two or three times, the matter in hand became so knotty, that the jackal found it imperative on him to get up, and steep his towels anew. From these pilgrimages to the jug and basin, he returned with such eccentricities of damp headgear as no words can describe; which were made the more ludicrous by his anxious gravity.

The jackal, though, was focused on his work, his face serious, so deep in thought he often forgot his glass. He'd search for it for a minute or two before finding it. Sometimes the work was too tough, and he'd get up to get more water. When he came back, he put on strange, wet headgear that looked even worse with his serious face. It showed how different they were, how their personalities shaped what they did.

title: A Tale of Two Cities
input: The speaker expresses deep regret for causing a situation and requests someone to convey their sincere apologies to another person. Mr. Carton displays a careless demeanor, bordering on insolence, as he leans against the bar, partially turned away from the prisoner. He suggests that expecting a certain outcome is wise and likely, but also indicates that their withdrawal may actually benefit the situation. Jerry, unable to linger outside the courtroom, departs without hearing further conversation. He observes the two individuals standing side by side, noting that while they share similar features, their manners are quite different, as reflected in the glass above them.
human:
“I am deeply sorry to have been the cause of it. Could you tell her so for me, with my fervent acknowledgments?”

Mr. Carton’s manner was so careless as to be almost insolent. He stood, half turned from the prisoner, lounging with his elbow against the bar.

“It’s the wisest thing to expect, and the likeliest. But I think their withdrawing is in your favour.”

Loitering on the way out of court not being allowed, Jerry heard no more: but left them - so like each other in feature, so unlike each other in manner - standing side by side, both reflected in the glass above them.

“Ah, but I am sorry to have given you a little trouble. Let me tell this to you in my name. And now, if you will be so good as to say to him that I am sorry to have given him a little trouble, you will make me very happy.”

Mr. Carton, lounging lazily against the bar, his back turned half-way towards the prisoner, made a careless gesture of defiance, and said, “That’s wise, and likely. But your withdrawal will do them good.”

Jerry could not stay outside the courtroom. He left without hearing the rest. He saw the two men standing, side by side, and noticed that they were very much alike, except that their manners were very different, as shown by the glass over their heads.

title: A Tale of Two Cities
input:
He gazed at her with a fearful expression, and after a moment, his lips began to form words, although no sound was audible. As he paused between breaths, which were rapid and labored, he was eventually heard to speak.

Meanwhile, tears streamed down her face, and she brought her hands to her lips, kissing them as a gesture to him. Subsequently, she clasped her hands to her breast, as if she were cradling his injured head.

She did not yet trust her voice, so she sat down beside him on the bench. However, he recoiled from her, but she gently placed her hand on his arm. This action caused a strange sensation to pass through him, which was visible in his physical reaction. Consequently, he laid the knife down quietly, continuing to stare at her.
